description: How a program becomes electrons: lexing and parsing, type systems, IR and optimisation, codegen, ABI and linking, interpreters, JITs and GC, x86-64 / ARM64 / RISC-V / IBM Z assembly, pipelines, out-of-order cores and microcode, caches and memory models, GPU SIMT, TPU systolic arrays and ML compilers, and the explicit mapping between all these layers. For a cloud/enterprise architect who programs and wants a lasting, zero-to-hero mental model of compilers, ISAs and accelerators.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::01 Lexing & Parsing
notes.front: Why do compilers split the front end into a lexer and a parser instead of one pass over characters?
notes.back: Tokens are a regular language (fast deterministic finite automaton (DFA), no stack); structure is context-free. Splitting keeps the grammar free of whitespace/comment noise and makes each part simpler and faster.
notes.analogy: Reading: you first group letters into words, then words into sentences. Nobody parses grammar letter by letter.
notes.extra: In practice: the lexer discards whitespace and comments, so the grammar never has to mention them.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::01 Lexing & Parsing
notes.text: Lexer construction: regular expression → {{c1::NFA (Thompson's construction)}} → {{c2::DFA (subset construction)}} → {{c3::minimised DFA}} → a transition table the lexer walks one character at a time.
notes.extra: Example: flex, re2c and most regex engines used for lexing do exactly this; backtracking engines (PCRE) do not.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::01 Lexing & Parsing
notes.front: Why does a lexer run a DFA rather than simulating the nondeterministic finite automaton (NFA) directly?
notes.back: A deterministic finite automaton (DFA) is in exactly one state, so each character is one table lookup: O(1) per character, no backtracking, no set of states to track.
notes.analogy: NFA simulation is like following every fork in a maze at once; the DFA has pre-computed where each combination of forks leads.
notes.extra: Pitfall: subset construction can blow up to 2n states in the worst case, which is why lexer generators minimise and compress the table.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::01 Lexing & Parsing
notes.front: What is the maximal munch (longest match) rule, and what does it do to a+++b?
notes.back: The lexer always takes the longest prefix that forms a token. So a+++b becomes a ++ + b, never a + ++b.
notes.extra: Pitfall: C++ vector<vector<int>> lexed as >>; C++11 made the parser split the token when a template argument list is being closed.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::01 Lexing & Parsing
notes.front: What is the C lexer hack, and why is it needed for foo * bar;?
notes.back: The statement is a multiplication if foo is a variable but a pointer declaration if it is a typedef. The parser feeds declared typedef names back to the lexer, which then emits TYPE_NAME instead of IDENT.
notes.analogy: The sentence "Buffalo buffalo" only parses once you know which word is a noun; the lexer is told by the parser which names are types.
notes.extra: Link: 02 Types · symbol table

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::01 Lexing & Parsing
notes.front: How does Python's lexer turn significant whitespace into tokens a context-free grammar can use?
notes.back: It keeps a stack of indentation widths and emits virtual INDENT/DEDENT tokens when a line is indented more or less than the stack top. The grammar then treats them like { and }.
notes.extra: Pitfall: inside brackets the lexer suppresses NEWLINE/INDENT entirely, which is why a multi-line list literal needs no backslashes.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::01 Lexing & Parsing
notes.front: What can a context-free grammar express that a regular expression cannot?
notes.back: Unbounded nesting: balanced parentheses, nested blocks, expressions inside expressions. A regex has no memory (no stack) to remember how many openers are pending.
notes.analogy: A regex is a turnstile that only sees the current person; a CFG has a stack of IOUs it can pay back later.
notes.extra: Example: that is why "parse HTML with regex" is a joke: tags nest.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::01 Lexing & Parsing
notes.front: What makes a grammar ambiguous, and why is that a problem for a compiler?
notes.back: Some input has two or more parse trees. The compiler would have two meanings for one program (e.g. 1 - 2 - 3 as (1-2)-3 or 1-(2-3)).
notes.extra: Example: the dangling else: if a if b x else y: does else belong to the inner or outer if? Most languages bind it to the nearest if, which is exactly what yacc/bison's default (shift on a shift/reduce conflict) produces.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::01 Lexing & Parsing
notes.text: To encode precedence in a grammar you give each level its own nonterminal: expr → expr + term | term, term → term * factor | factor; the operator {{c1::lower in the grammar (closer to the leaves)}} binds tighter. Left associativity comes from {{c2::left-recursive}} rules like expr → expr + term.
notes.extra: In practice: yacc/bison let you keep an ambiguous grammar and add %left '+', %left '*' declarations to resolve conflicts instead.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::01 Lexing & Parsing
notes.front: Why can a top-down (recursive descent) parser not handle the left-recursive rule expr → expr + term directly?
notes.back: To parse expr it first calls expr without consuming any input: infinite recursion. Rewrite as expr → term (+ term)*, i.e. a loop.
notes.extra: Contrast: Left-to-right, rightmost-derivation (LR) parsers love left recursion (constant stack depth); right recursion makes their stack grow with the list length.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::01 Lexing & Parsing
notes.front: What is a recursive descent parser, structurally?
notes.back: One function per nonterminal; each function looks at the next token(s) to choose an alternative, calls the functions for the rule's symbols and consumes terminals. The call stack is the parse stack.
notes.extra: Why loved: plain code, easy to debug, trivial to add context-sensitive checks and good error messages.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::01 Lexing & Parsing
notes.front: What does the (1) in LL(1) mean, and what does it demand of the grammar?
notes.back: One token of lookahead decides which alternative to take. Alternatives of a rule must therefore start with disjoint token sets (no common prefixes, no left recursion).
notes.extra: In practice: hand-written parsers cheat with unlimited lookahead or backtracking where left-to-right, leftmost-derivation (LL)(1) is inconvenient; Python's old parser was LL(1) and accumulated hacks for that reason.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::01 Lexing & Parsing
notes.front: What is a Pratt parser (top-down operator precedence), and why is it the standard way to hand-write expression parsing?
notes.back: A loop with binding powers: parse a prefix, then while the next operator's left binding power exceeds the current minimum, consume it and recursively parse its right side. Precedence and associativity become numbers, not grammar levels.
notes.analogy: Each operator is a magnet with a strength; an operand sticks to whichever neighbour pulls harder.
notes.extra: In practice: used in rustc, Go, Roslyn, Crafting Interpreters' clox. Right associativity = recurse with binding power minus one.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::01 Lexing & Parsing
notes.front: LL vs LR parsing: key difference?
notes.back: Left-to-right, leftmost-derivation (LL) is top-down: it must predict the rule from the first token(s). Left-to-right, rightmost-derivation (LR) is bottom-up: it shifts tokens onto a stack and only decides on a rule after seeing its whole right-hand side (plus lookahead). LR accepts strictly more grammars.
notes.analogy: LL guesses the dish from the first ingredient; LR tastes the whole plate, then names it.
notes.extra: Mnemonic: LL = Left-to-right scan, Leftmost derivation; LR = Left-to-right scan, Rightmost derivation in reverse.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::01 Lexing & Parsing
notes.front: In an LR (shift-reduce) parser, what do shift and reduce do?
notes.back: Shift pushes the next input token onto the stack. Reduce pops a rule's right-hand side off the stack and pushes its nonterminal. A table indexed by (state, lookahead) says which to do.
notes.extra: Example: with E + T on the stack and lookahead *, the table says shift, which is exactly how * ends up binding tighter than +.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::01 Lexing & Parsing
notes.text: Left-to-right, rightmost-derivation (LR) table flavours: {{c1::SLR}} uses FOLLOW sets for reduce decisions (small, weak); {{c2::canonical LR(1)}} carries a lookahead in every item (strongest, huge tables); {{c3::LALR(1)}} merges LR(1) states with the same core, nearly as strong with SLR-sized tables, and is what yacc/bison build.
notes.extra: Pitfall: merging states can introduce reduce/reduce conflicts that LR(1) would not have, a classic head-scratcher when bison rejects a grammar.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::01 Lexing & Parsing
notes.front: What does a GLR parser do when the left-to-right, rightmost-derivation (LR) table has a conflict?
notes.back: It forks the parse stack and pursues every action in parallel (sharing common prefixes); branches that hit an error die, and surviving branches merge again. Ambiguity becomes a parse forest instead of an error.
notes.analogy: A detective who follows every suspect simultaneously and drops those whose alibi checks out.
notes.extra: Example: tree-sitter and Elkhound (a C++ parser) are generalised LR (GLR); it handles C++'s declaration-vs-expression ambiguity without the lexer hack.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::01 Lexing & Parsing
notes.front: Why are the parsers of clang, GCC, rustc and Go hand-written instead of generated by yacc/bison/ANTLR?
notes.back: Hand-written recursive descent gives precise error messages and recovery, easy context-sensitive hacks (typedefs, templates, >>), and faster code. Generated tables are rigid and their error handling is poor.
notes.extra: In practice: GNU Compiler Collection (GCC) moved from a bison grammar to hand-written C parsers around 2004 for exactly these reasons. Generators remain great for prototypes, domain-specific languages (DSLs) and verifying a grammar is unambiguous.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::01 Lexing & Parsing
notes.front: What is panic-mode error recovery, and why do parsers want to recover at all?
notes.back: On an error, discard tokens until a synchronising token (;, }, a statement keyword), then continue. The goal is to report many real errors per run while avoiding cascades of bogus follow-on errors.
notes.extra: In practice: IDEs need even more: the tree must stay usable while the user is mid-keystroke, which is why tree-sitter inserts explicit ERROR/MISSING nodes rather than aborting.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::01 Lexing & Parsing
notes.front: Parse tree (concrete syntax tree) vs AST: key difference?
notes.back: The parse tree mirrors the grammar exactly, including every nonterminal, parenthesis and semicolon. The abstract syntax tree (AST) keeps only meaning: (1 + 2) is just a + node with two children.
notes.analogy: A verbatim court transcript (parse tree) versus the minutes that record the decisions (AST).
notes.extra: Link: 03 IR & Optimisation · AST → IR

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::01 Lexing & Parsing
notes.front: How does a PEG grammar avoid ambiguity, and what is the cost?
notes.back: Alternatives are ordered (/): the first one that matches wins and later ones are never tried. So there is never more than one parse, but the grammar may silently fail to accept inputs you meant.
notes.extra: Pitfall: A ← 'a' / 'ab' never matches ab; with context-free grammar (CFG) alternation it would. Put the longer alternative first. Packrat: memoising every (rule, position) makes parsing expression grammar (PEG) backtracking linear; CPython's parser (PEP 617) is PEG/packrat.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::01 Lexing & Parsing
notes.front: How does incremental parsing (tree-sitter) make re-parsing a 10 000-line file after one keystroke cheap?
notes.back: The editor reports the edited byte range; the parser reuses every subtree of the old tree that the edit cannot have touched and re-parses only the affected region. Cost scales with the edit, not the file.
notes.analogy: Repairing one brick in a wall instead of rebuilding the wall.
notes.extra: In practice: that is what powers syntax highlighting, folding and structural navigation in Neovim, Zed, GitHub and many Language Server Protocol (LSP) tools.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::01 Lexing & Parsing
notes.front: A compiler's lexer tokens vs an LLM's BPE tokens: key difference?
notes.back: A lexer's tokens are defined by the language grammar (one identifier, one keyword). Byte-pair encoding (BPE) tokens are statistically frequent byte sequences: printf( may be one token and xyzzy three, with no notion of syntax.
notes.extra: In practice: this is why LLMs mis-count characters and struggle with unusual identifiers, and why code tools like tree-sitter are used to give models syntax-aware chunks.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::01 Lexing & Parsing
notes.front: Why can C++ syntax not be parsed without semantic information, e.g. T(x); or a<b>(c)?
notes.back: The same token sequence is a declaration, a cast or a comparison depending on what T, a and b were declared as. The parser must consult the symbol table (and even instantiate templates) while parsing.
notes.extra: Example: the "most vexing parse": Widget w(Gadget()); declares a function, not an object. Link: 02 Types · symbol table

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::02 Semantic Analysis & Type Systems
notes.front: What is a symbol table, and which questions does it let the compiler answer that the grammar cannot?
notes.back: A map from a name to what the compiler knows about it: kind (variable, function, type), type, storage, declaring scope. It answers context-dependent questions: is this name declared and visible, do operand types fit, is this const being assigned?
notes.extra: Link: 04 Codegen & ABI · register allocation

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::02 Semantic Analysis & Type Systems
notes.front: How does a compiler implement nested block scopes and shadowing?
notes.back: A chain (stack) of symbol tables: entering a block pushes a table, leaving pops it; lookup walks from the innermost outward and stops at the first hit, so inner declarations shadow outer ones.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::02 Semantic Analysis & Type Systems
notes.front: Lexical (static) vs dynamic scope: key difference?
notes.back: Lexical: a free variable refers to the binding in the enclosing source text, fixed at compile time. Dynamic: it refers to the most recent binding on the call stack at run time, so meaning depends on the caller.
notes.analogy: Lexical: your surname is set by where you were born. Dynamic: you take the surname of whoever you are currently visiting.
notes.extra: Example: almost all modern languages are lexical; Emacs Lisp (historically) and Bash's local are dynamic. Lexical scope is what makes closures and separate compilation work.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::02 Semantic Analysis & Type Systems
notes.front: Why can a compiler for a lexically scoped language turn every variable reference into a fixed slot index before the program runs?
notes.back: Because the binding each name refers to is decided by source nesting alone. A resolver pass walks the scopes once and records (depth, index); run-time lookup is then an array access, not a hash lookup by name.
notes.extra: Example: Crafting Interpreters' resolver pass; CPython's compiler classifies names as local/global/cell and emits LOAD_FAST vs LOAD_GLOBAL. Link: 05 Runtimes · bytecode & slot indices

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::02 Semantic Analysis & Type Systems
notes.front: What is a closure, and what problem forces a compiler to treat it specially?
notes.back: A function value bundled with the environment it was created in. The problem: it may outlive the stack frame that holds its captured variables, so those variables cannot simply live on the stack.
notes.analogy: A letter that carries its own return address even after the writer has moved house.
notes.extra: Mechanism (Lua, clox): a captured variable stays in its stack slot as an open upvalue and is copied to the heap (closed) only when the frame returns, so locals that never escape stay cheap.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::02 Semantic Analysis & Type Systems
notes.front: Static vs dynamic typing: key difference?
notes.back: Static: types belong to expressions and are checked before the program runs (C, Rust, Java). Dynamic: types belong to run-time values and are checked when an operation executes (Python, JavaScript (JS)).
notes.extra: Pitfall: "strongly typed" is a fuzzy marketing term; say static/dynamic and sound/unsound instead. Link: 05 Runtimes · speculation removes dynamic checks

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::02 Semantic Analysis & Type Systems
notes.front: Why can a type checker not be both sound and complete for a general-purpose language?
notes.back: Whether a program ever misuses a value is undecidable (Rice's theorem), so the checker must approximate. Sound systems err by rejecting good programs; complete ones err by accepting bad ones. Languages choose soundness and add escape hatches (casts, unsafe).
notes.analogy: Airport security: a sound scanner never lets a weapon through, at the price of confiscating some harmless water bottles.
notes.extra: Definition: sound = every program the checker accepts cannot fail with a type error at run time. ML and safe Rust are sound; TypeScript and Java arrays are deliberately unsound for ergonomics or history.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::02 Semantic Analysis & Type Systems
notes.front: Why is Java's array covariance (String[] is an Object[]) unsound, and how does Java cope?
notes.back: Object[] a = new String[1]; a[0] = 1; type-checks but stores an Integer in a String array. Java inserts a run-time check that throws ArrayStoreException.
notes.extra: Lesson: a mutable container can only be safely covariant if it is read-only; generics (List<String>) are therefore invariant.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::02 Semantic Analysis & Type Systems
notes.front: Type checking vs type inference: key difference?
notes.back: Checking verifies that annotated types are consistent (programmer supplies types, compiler says yes/no). Inference computes types the programmer left out, usually by generating and solving constraints.
notes.extra: In practice: most languages do both: Rust and TypeScript infer locals but require signatures on functions, which keeps error messages local and compilation modular.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::02 Semantic Analysis & Type Systems
notes.front: What is bidirectional type checking, and why do modern checkers (Rust, Swift, TypeScript, Haskell) use it?
notes.back: Two modes: check an expression against an expected type (information flows down), or synthesise a type from the expression (flows up). Annotations are needed only where synthesis is impossible, e.g. lambda parameters.
notes.analogy: Filling a form: some fields you work out yourself; others are pre-printed and you only confirm they fit.
notes.extra: Why: it scales to features full Hindley-Milner (HM) cannot handle (subtyping, higher-rank types) and gives errors at the annotation that was violated.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::02 Semantic Analysis & Type Systems
notes.front: What does Hindley–Milner inference guarantee, and what is its core algorithm?
notes.back: Every well-typed expression has a principal (most general) type, found without annotations. Core: assign fresh type variables, collect equality constraints from each application, solve them by unification.
notes.extra: Example: ML, OCaml, Haskell (core), Rust (within one function body), and the type inference in Elm and F#.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::02 Semantic Analysis & Type Systems
notes.front: What does unification compute, and what is the occurs check for?
notes.back: The most general substitution making two types equal: unify a → int with bool → b gives a = bool, b = int. The occurs check rejects a = a → b, which would be an infinite type.
notes.analogy: Solving simultaneous equations where the unknowns are types.
notes.extra: Example: the occurs check is what rejects f x = x x in ML: x would need type a and a → b at once.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::02 Semantic Analysis & Type Systems
notes.front: What is let-polymorphism, and why does Hindley-Milner (HM) generalise at let but not at lambda parameters?
notes.back: A let-bound definition gets a type scheme (∀a. a → a) and can be used at several types in its body. Generalising lambda parameters too would be System F, whose inference is undecidable.
notes.extra: Example: let id = fun x -> x in (id 1, id true) is fine; passing id as a lambda argument and using it at two types is not.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::02 Semantic Analysis & Type Systems
notes.front: Why does ML need the value restriction (generalise only syntactic values)?
notes.back: let r = ref [] would get type ∀a. a list ref; then r := [1] and !r : bool list both type-check: unsound. Only values (lambdas, constants) are generalised, so ref [] stays monomorphic.
notes.analogy: A blank cheque (polymorphic) must not be issued for a box whose contents can be swapped after the fact.
notes.extra: Lesson: polymorphism and mutation interact badly; this is the same root cause as Java's array covariance problem.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::02 Semantic Analysis & Type Systems
notes.text: Variance of a function type: A → B is {{c1::contravariant}} in its argument (accepts a wider input) and {{c2::covariant}} in its result (returns a narrower output). A mutable cell or array must be {{c3::invariant}} to stay sound.
notes.analogy: A job posting: a candidate who accepts more kinds of tasks (wider input) and delivers more specific results (narrower output) is a safe substitute.
notes.extra: Contrast: subtyping (one type stands in for another) is a different mechanism from Hindley-Milner (HM) polymorphism (one body for all types). Example: Kotlin's out T/in T, Java's ? extends/? super, Rust's lifetime variance all express this.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::02 Semantic Analysis & Type Systems
notes.front: Nominal vs structural typing: key difference?
notes.back: Nominal: compatibility is by declared name/inheritance (Java classes, Rust structs). Structural: by shape, i.e. having the right members (TypeScript interfaces, Go interfaces, OCaml objects).
notes.extra: Pitfall: structural typing lets two unrelated types with the same fields be confused (Metres vs Feet); newtype wrappers restore nominal distinctions.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::02 Semantic Analysis & Type Systems
notes.front: Implementing generics: monomorphisation vs erasure / dictionary passing: key difference?
notes.back: Monomorphisation (C++ templates, Rust) emits a specialised copy per type argument. Erasure (Java) compiles one body over boxed values; dictionary passing (Haskell, Swift witness tables) compiles one body plus a hidden table of operations.
notes.analogy: Printing a separate manual per customer language (monomorphisation) versus one manual with an interpreter on call (dictionary).

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::02 Semantic Analysis & Type Systems
notes.front: What do you gain and what do you pay with monomorphisation?
notes.back: Gain: no boxing, no indirect calls, each copy is inlined and optimised for its concrete type. Pay: code bloat, long compile times, and every generic definition must be visible at the use site (no separate compilation of generic bodies).
notes.extra: Link: 03 IR & Optimisation · inlining heuristics; 09 Memory · i-cache footprint

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::02 Semantic Analysis & Type Systems
notes.front: How does a trait / typeclass constraint like T: Display or Show a => become machine code?
notes.back: Either the compiler monomorphises (Rust generics: direct calls), or it passes a dictionary: a record of function pointers for that type, i.e. a vtable supplied as a hidden argument (Haskell, Swift, Rust dyn Trait).
notes.extra: Example: Rust gives you both: fn f<T: Trait> (static, monomorphised) vs fn f(x: &dyn Trait) (dynamic, fat pointer = data ptr + vtable ptr). Link: 03 IR & Optimisation · devirtualisation

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::02 Semantic Analysis & Type Systems
notes.front: What is gradual typing, and what does TypeScript give up compared with a sound gradual system?
notes.back: A dynamic type (any) that is "consistent" with every type, letting typed and untyped code mix. Sound gradual typing inserts run-time casts at the boundary (and can blame the untyped side); TypeScript erases all types, so a wrong any fails somewhere far away.
notes.extra: In practice: the boundary checks cost performance (Typed Racket, Python's typeguard), which is why most industrial gradual systems skip them.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::02 Semantic Analysis & Type Systems
notes.front: In one card: what does Rust's borrow checker prove, and how?
notes.back: Aliasing XOR mutation: at any point a value has either one &mut or any number of &, and no reference outlives its owner. It computes each borrow's lifetime from use sites (non-lexical lifetimes) and rejects overlapping conflicting borrows.
notes.extra: Link: 05 Runtimes · Rust ownership vs GC; Deep C · memory errors

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::02 Semantic Analysis & Type Systems
notes.front: In one card: what are dependent types, and what do they buy?
notes.back: Types that mention values: Vec n a is a list of length n, so append : Vec n a → Vec m a → Vec (n+m) a. Properties become types and programs become proofs (Idris, Agda, Lean, Coq).
notes.extra: Cost: type checking may need to evaluate programs and can require manual proofs; mainstream languages borrow the idea in weaker forms (Rust const generics, TypeScript literal types).

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::02 Semantic Analysis & Type Systems
notes.front: What is desugaring (lowering), and why does a compiler do it right after type checking?
notes.back: Rewriting convenience syntax into a smaller core language: for → while over an iterator, a += b → a = a + b, async → a state machine. Later passes then handle a few constructs instead of dozens.
notes.analogy: Translating a rich dialect into a small pidgin everyone downstream understands.
notes.extra: Example: rustc lowers abstract syntax tree (AST) → HIR (desugared) → MIR (control flow graph). Link: 03 IR & Optimisation · IR designs (LLVM IR / MIR)

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::02 Semantic Analysis & Type Systems
notes.front: How does undefined behaviour fit into a language's semantics, and why do compilers treat it as licence rather than as an error?
notes.back: The spec defines the meaning of programs only when no UB occurs; a program that triggers UB has no defined meaning. The optimiser may therefore assume UB never happens and transform the program under that assumption.
notes.analogy: A contract that says "if you break clause 7, nothing else in this contract applies".
notes.extra: Link: 03 IR & Optimisation · undef vs poison; Deep C · UB catalogue

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::03 IR & Optimisation
notes.front: Why do compilers lower the abstract syntax tree (AST) to an intermediate representation instead of optimising the tree directly?
notes.back: An IR is flat and explicit (temporaries, no nesting, uniform ops), so analyses are simple, and it decouples M front ends from N back ends: M+N components instead of M×N.
notes.analogy: A hub airport: every city flies to the hub and the hub flies everywhere, instead of a direct route between every pair of cities.
notes.extra: Form: three-address code: one operator and at most three operands per instruction, nested expressions flattened into temporaries (a = b*c + d → t1 = b*c; a = t1 + d). In practice: clang, rustc, Swift, Julia and Zig all target LLVM IR.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::03 IR & Optimisation
notes.front: Abstract syntax tree (AST) → intermediate representation (IR): what is lost in the lowering, and what is gained?
notes.back: Lost: source structure (nesting, parentheses, sugar, names of sub-expressions) and the easy path to good error messages; positions survive only as debug metadata. Gained: explicit control flow (CFG), explicit temporaries and one uniform instruction set, so analyses become graph algorithms.
notes.analogy: From a novel to a flowchart: the prose is gone, but the plot logic is finally explicit.
notes.extra: In practice: that is why type errors are reported on the AST and missed-optimisation remarks (-Rpass-missed) on the IR. Link: 01 Parsing · parse tree vs AST; 02 Types · desugaring

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::03 IR & Optimisation
notes.front: What is a basic block, and why does the optimiser split code into them?
notes.back: A maximal straight-line sequence: entered only at its first instruction, left only at its last. Inside a block there is no control flow, so local analysis is trivial; all the hard reasoning moves to the edges between blocks.
notes.extra: In practice: a block starts at a leader: the function entry, any branch target, or the instruction after a branch. Blocks plus edges form the control-flow graph; a loop is a back edge. Link: 08 Microarchitecture · branch prediction

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::03 IR & Optimisation
notes.front: Why do virtually all modern optimisers work on static single assignment (SSA) form?
notes.back: Each value is assigned exactly once, so every use points at its single definition. Def-use chains come for free and constant propagation, global value numbering (GVN) and dead-code elimination (DCE) become sparse (work per value, not per program point) and much simpler.
notes.analogy: Immutable variables in a functional language, or Git commits: nothing is ever overwritten, you just create a new name for the new value.
notes.extra: Example: x = 1; x = x + 1 becomes x1 = 1; x2 = x1 + 1.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::03 IR & Optimisation
notes.text: In static single assignment (SSA), a {{c1::φ-function}} sits at the start of a join block and selects, for each incoming {{c2::predecessor edge}}, which version of the variable flows in, e.g. x4 = φ(x2 from B1, x3 from B2).
notes.analogy: A railway points switch at a junction: the value that arrives depends on which track you came in on.
notes.extra: Pitfall: φ is not an instruction the CPU runs: before code generation each φ becomes copies at the end of its predecessor blocks, which the register allocator then coalesces away. Link: 04 Codegen & ABI · register allocation (φ → copies)

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::03 IR & Optimisation
notes.front: In a control-flow graph (CFG), what does “A dominates B” mean?
notes.back: Every path from the entry block to B passes through A. The entry dominates everything; every block dominates itself. The relation forms the dominator tree.
notes.analogy: A toll booth on the only road into a valley: whatever is true at the booth is true everywhere in the valley.
notes.extra: In practice: a definition in A is guaranteed visible in every block A dominates, which is why dominance underlies static single assignment (SSA), loop-invariant code motion (LICM) and global value numbering (GVN).

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::03 IR & Optimisation
notes.front: Where does classic static single assignment (SSA) construction (Cytron et al.) place φ-functions for a variable defined in block A?
notes.back: In A's dominance frontier: blocks B that A does not strictly dominate but one of whose predecessors A does dominate. Iterate, because a new φ is itself a definition.
notes.extra: Example: in the picture DF(B1) = DF(B2) = {B3}, so B3 gets one φ. Also: this gives minimal SSA; pruned SSA additionally drops φs for dead variables (needs liveness). Braun et al. 2013 build SSA straight from the abstract syntax tree (AST) without dominance frontiers.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::03 IR & Optimisation
notes.front: What is dataflow analysis in one sentence, and how is the answer computed?
notes.back: A per-block transfer function plus a meet operator over a lattice; iterate over the control-flow graph (CFG) until nothing changes (fixpoint). Monotone functions on a finite-height lattice guarantee termination.
notes.analogy: Rumours spreading through an office: each person combines what their neighbours know and passes it on, until a day goes by with nothing new.
notes.extra: Direction: forward analyses ask what may have happened before a point (reaching definitions, constants); backward ones ask what will be needed after it (liveness).

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::03 IR & Optimisation
notes.front: When is a variable live at a program point, and who consumes that fact?
notes.back: If some path from that point reaches a use before any redefinition. Register allocation needs it: two values whose live ranges overlap interfere and cannot share a register.
notes.extra: Also: dead-store elimination is just “a store to something not live is useless”. Link: 04 Codegen & ABI · interference graph

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::03 IR & Optimisation
notes.front: Why does SCCP (sparse conditional constant propagation) find constants that alternating constant propagation and dead-code elimination miss?
notes.back: It is optimistic: it assumes every edge unreachable and every value a constant until proven otherwise, so a branch whose condition becomes constant never feeds “unknown” values into the join.
notes.analogy: Assume innocence and only convict on evidence, instead of assuming everyone guilty until cleared: you convict far fewer values of being “unknown”.
notes.extra: Example: x = 1; if (x > 0) y = 2; else y = 3; → SCCP proves y == 2 because the else edge is never executable (Wegman–Zadeck 1991).

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::03 IR & Optimisation
notes.front: CSE vs GVN: what does global value numbering catch that common-subexpression elimination doesn't?
notes.back: CSE matches lexically identical expressions. GVN assigns a number to each value computed, so it also catches a+b vs b+a, copies and renamed variables, and (with partial redundancy elimination (PRE)) expressions available on only some paths.
notes.extra: In practice: LLVM runs EarlyCSE cheaply and often, and GVN/NewGVN once in the main pipeline.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::03 IR & Optimisation
notes.front: Why is inlining called the most important optimisation, even though a call is cheap?
notes.back: Not for the saved call: it exposes the callee's body to the caller's context, so constants propagate, branches die, loads and stores can be matched, and everything else can then fire.
notes.analogy: Unwrapping a sealed parcel: only once the contents are visible can you throw away the packaging you don't need.
notes.extra: Link: 05 Runtimes · speculative inlining through inline caches

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::03 IR & Optimisation
notes.front: What does an inlining heuristic weigh, and what breaks when it inlines too much?
notes.back: A cost estimate of the callee after simplification (bonuses for constant arguments, hot call sites, single callers) against a threshold that rises with -O3 and falls with -Os. Too much: code bloat, i-cache misses, slower compiles.
notes.extra: In practice: always_inline/noinline override the heuristic; recursion and indirect calls block it. Link: 09 Memory · i-cache & cache lines

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::03 IR & Optimisation
notes.front: What does LICM do, and what two things must it prove before hoisting a computation?
notes.back: Loop-invariant code motion moves computations whose operands don't change in the loop into the preheader. It must prove the operands are invariant and that executing it on every entry is safe (no trap, no aliasing store).
notes.extra: Pitfall: a load of a global looks invariant until some store through a pointer in the loop may alias it; then LICM needs alias analysis or gives up. Example: strlen(s) in a for condition is hoisted only if the body is proven not to modify s.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::03 IR & Optimisation
notes.front: What does loop unrolling buy, and what does it cost?
notes.back: Fewer branches and induction-variable updates per element, and a bigger straight-line body for scheduling and superword-level parallelism (SLP) vectorisation. Costs: code size, i-cache pressure and a remainder loop for trip counts not divisible by the factor.
notes.extra: Link: 08 Microarchitecture · loop-carried dependency

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::03 IR & Optimisation
notes.front: What does strength reduction turn the address computation of a[i] inside a loop into?
notes.back: A pointer that is incremented by sizeof(a[0]) each iteration, replacing a multiply with an add; the loop test is then rewritten to compare the pointer against an end address (linear-function test replacement).
notes.analogy: Instead of computing “row 1 × 8 metres” each time, you just take eight more steps from where you stood.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::03 IR & Optimisation
notes.front: Loop vectorisation vs SLP vectorisation: what is the difference?
notes.back: Loop: widen a loop body so one vector instruction handles several consecutive iterations. SLP (superword-level parallelism): pack similar independent scalar operations within straight-line code into one vector op, no loop needed.
notes.extra: Example: r.x = a.x+b.x; r.y = a.y+b.y; is an SLP candidate. Also: when pointers might overlap, the loop vectoriser emits runtime range checks and keeps a scalar fallback (versioning); restrict removes both. Link: 06 x86-64 · ymm/zmm registers

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::03 IR & Optimisation
notes.front: Why won't for (...) sum += a[i]; with float sum vectorise at -O3 without -ffast-math (or -fassociative-math)?
notes.back: A vector reduction adds the elements in a different order (several partial sums), and floating-point addition is not associative, so the result could differ in the last bits. The compiler is not allowed to change observable results.
notes.extra: In practice: clang's -Rpass-missed=loop-vectorize or gcc's -fopt-info-vec-missed tells you exactly why a loop was skipped; #pragma omp simd reduction is the surgical opt-in.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::03 IR & Optimisation
notes.front: How does type-based alias analysis reach the optimiser in LLVM, given LLVM intermediate representation (IR) has no C types?
notes.back: The front end attaches !tbaa metadata to every load and store, describing the access type in a type tree; the alias analysis then reports that accesses of unrelated types cannot alias.
notes.extra: Pitfall: this is exactly why -fno-strict-aliasing is a front-end flag: it just stops emitting the metadata. Link: Deep C · strict aliasing

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::03 IR & Optimisation
notes.front: When can a compiler devirtualise a C++ virtual call into a direct (and then inlinable) call?
notes.back: When it knows the dynamic type: the object was just constructed in view, the class or method is final, or whole-program vtable analysis (link-time optimisation (LTO), -fwhole-program-vtables) shows a single override.
notes.extra: Also: with profile data it can speculatively devirtualise: if (vptr == Expected) inlined_body(); else indirect_call();. Link: 05 Runtimes · inline caches

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::03 IR & Optimisation
notes.text: Profile-guided optimisation (PGO) feeds real execution counts back into the compiler. {{c1::Instrumented}} PGO inserts counters into a special build (exact, but slower training runs); {{c2::sampling}} PGO (AutoFDO) uses perf samples from production binaries (approximate, zero build friction).
notes.extra: In practice: profiles mostly change block layout (hot path straight-line, cold code moved away), inlining decisions and branch probabilities; typical wins are 5–15% on branchy code.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::03 IR & Optimisation
notes.front: LLVM undef vs poison: what is the difference?
notes.back: undef: an arbitrary ordinary value (each use may pick a different one). poison: the result of violating a rule such as nsw; it propagates through arithmetic and is undefined behaviour (UB) only once it reaches a side effect.
notes.extra: In practice: freeze pins poison to one arbitrary value. Example of UB exploitation: after *p on every path, a later if (p == NULL) is deleted (kernel: -fno-delete-null-pointer-checks). Link: Deep C · UB catalogue

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::03 IR & Optimisation
notes.text: Three intermediate representation (IR) designs: {{c1::LLVM IR}} is a single typed static single assignment (SSA) language, close to a portable assembler; {{c2::GCC}} lowers through GENERIC → GIMPLE (three-address, SSA) → RTL (target-specific); {{c3::MLIR}} is a framework of dialects at different abstraction levels that are progressively lowered.
notes.extra: Link: 11 Accelerators · MLIR dialects

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::03 IR & Optimisation
notes.front: Why does an optimisation pipeline run cheap canonicalisation passes (InstCombine, SimplifyCFG, EarlyCSE) repeatedly between the expensive ones?
notes.back: Expensive passes pattern-match on a canonical shape (e.g. constants on the right, loops with a preheader and single latch). Each big pass leaves debris, so cleanup restores the shape the next pass expects.
notes.extra: Also: which pass runs when is the phase-ordering problem; -O2 is a hand-tuned sequence, not a search.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::03 IR & Optimisation
notes.text: Optimisation levels: {{c1::-O0}} no optimisation, debuggable; {{c2::-O2}} the production default (nearly everything but code-growing passes); {{c3::-O3}} adds aggressive inlining, unrolling and vectorisation thresholds; {{c4::-Os/-Oz}} optimise for size; {{c5::-Og}} optimise without hurting debugging.
notes.extra: Pitfall: -O3 is not always faster than -O2: bigger code can lose in the i-cache. Measure.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::03 IR & Optimisation
notes.front: In -O2 output a static helper function has vanished from objdump and from the symbol table. What happened, and how do you confirm it?
notes.back: It was inlined into all callers and, being internal, deleted. Confirm with -Rpass=inline (clang) or -fopt-info-inline (gcc), or read the intermediate representation (IR) with -emit-llvm -S.
notes.extra: In practice: Compiler Explorer with -O2 -emit-llvm or GNU Compiler Collection (GCC)'s -fdump-tree-optimized shows the IR after the middle end, before instruction selection. Link: 06 x86-64 · reading compiler output

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::04 Code Generation, ABI & Linking
notes.front: Why is instruction selection described as tiling a tree or directed acyclic graph (DAG)?
notes.back: One machine instruction can cover several intermediate representation (IR) operations (x86 lea does shift+add+add; a memory operand folds a load into an add). The selector covers the IR graph with instruction patterns at minimum total cost.
notes.analogy: Covering a floor plan with rugs of different shapes and prices: the cheapest full cover is the chosen instruction sequence.
notes.extra: Example: a[i] + 4 → a single add rax, [rdi + rsi*4 + 4]. Link: 06 x86-64 · addressing modes

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::04 Code Generation, ABI & Linking
notes.front: What problem does register allocation solve, and what is the interference graph?
notes.back: Map unboundedly many virtual registers onto k physical ones. Nodes are live ranges; an edge joins two that are live at the same time and so cannot share a register. A valid allocation is a k-colouring.
notes.analogy: Hotel rooms (k of them) for guests with overlapping stays: two guests whose stays overlap cannot take the same room.
notes.extra: Link: 03 IR & Optimisation · liveness

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::04 Code Generation, ABI & Linking
notes.front: How does Chaitin–Briggs graph colouring decide which values to spill?
notes.back: Repeatedly remove any node with fewer than k neighbours (it can always be coloured later). When stuck, remove the node with the lowest spill cost per degree as a spill candidate. Colour in reverse order; candidates that find no colour are spilled.
notes.analogy: Seating guests who dislike each other at k tables: anyone with fewer than k enemies can always be seated last, so seat the troublemakers first.
notes.extra: Also: rematerialisation beats spilling for cheap values (constants, addresses): recompute at the use instead of store/reload.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::04 Code Generation, ABI & Linking
notes.front: Graph colouring vs linear scan register allocation: when is each chosen?
notes.back: Colouring: better code, superlinear time; ahead-of-time compilers. Linear scan: one pass over live intervals sorted by start, near-linear, slightly worse code; JITs (HotSpot C1, early V8) where compile time is on the critical path.
notes.extra: In practice: LLVM's default greedy allocator is a hybrid: global live ranges, priority queue, live-range splitting, with a fast allocator for -O0. Link: 05 Runtimes · tiered JIT

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::04 Code Generation, ABI & Linking
notes.front: Register allocation (compiler, 04) vs register renaming (core, 08): what does each map, and why are both needed?
notes.back: Allocation maps unbounded virtual registers onto the instruction set architecture (ISA)'s 16 or 31 names at compile time, spilling when short. Renaming maps those names onto hundreds of physical registers at run time, removing the false dependencies that name reuse created. The compiler decides what lives where; the core undoes the sharing.
notes.analogy: A hotel with 16 room numbers: allocation books guests into them; renaming quietly gives each new guest a fresh physical room while the number on the key stays the same.
notes.extra: Consequence: reusing a register for independent values is free, but partial-register merges and long dependency chains are not. Link: 08 Microarchitecture · register renaming; 06 x86-64 · partial-register writes

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::04 Code Generation, ABI & Linking
notes.front: Why does the back end still schedule instructions for a modern out-of-order CPU?
notes.back: The OoO window is finite and in-order cores (little cores, GPUs, embedded) need it badly; scheduling also hides latency of long ops, groups loads early and trades register pressure against parallelism (pre-RA vs post-RA scheduling).
notes.extra: Pitfall: aggressive pre-RA scheduling lengthens live ranges and causes spills, which is why LLVM schedules with a register-pressure model. Link: 08 Microarchitecture · scheduler (reservation stations)

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::04 Code Generation, ABI & Linking
notes.front: What does a calling convention fix, and why do application binary interfaces (ABIs) split registers into caller-saved and callee-saved?
notes.back: Where arguments and results go, register ownership, stack alignment, who cleans up. The split lets short-lived values use caller-saved registers for free, while values living across calls sit in callee-saved ones, saved only by functions that actually use them.
notes.extra: Link: Deep C · SysV argument registers & red zone; 06 x86-64 · call/ret

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::04 Code Generation, ABI & Linking
notes.front: SysV AMD64 vs Windows x64 calling convention: the key differences?
notes.back:
• 6 integer argument registers vs 4 (rcx, rdx, r8, r9)
  • Win64: caller reserves 32 bytes of shadow space; System V (SysV): none, but a red zone
  • Win64 keeps xmm6–15 callee-saved; SysV: all vector registers caller-saved
notes.extra: Why shadow space: the callee can spill its four register arguments to fixed slots next to the stack arguments, keeping varargs and unwinders simple. In practice: a Linux object cannot call a Windows DLL without a thunk. Link: 06 x86-64 · syscall vs function ABI

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::04 Code Generation, ABI & Linking
notes.text: AAPCS64 register roles: {{c1::x0–x7}} arguments and results; {{c2::x8}} indirect-result (struct return) pointer; {{c3::x16/x17}} intra-procedure scratch (IP0/IP1, used by PLT/veneers); {{c4::x18}} platform register (reserved by the OS); {{c5::x19–x28}} callee-saved; {{c6::x29}} frame pointer; {{c7::x30}} link register.
notes.extra: Link: 07 ARM64/RISC-V/Z · registers, sp, xzr

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::04 Code Generation, ABI & Linking
notes.front: How does the System V (SysV) AMD64 application binary interface (ABI) pass a small struct { double d; long n; } argument, and a 32-byte struct?
notes.back: Each eightbyte is classified: d is Streaming SIMD Extensions (SSE) → xmm0, n is INTEGER → rdi. Aggregates over 16 bytes (or with unaligned fields) are class MEMORY: copied onto the stack by the caller.
notes.extra: Pitfall: if registers run out midway through a struct, all its eightbytes go to the stack. Also: a large struct return uses a hidden pointer in rdi (sret), shifting the real arguments right.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::04 Code Generation, ABI & Linking
notes.front: Why is the x86-64 stack 16-byte aligned at every call, and what does that imply at function entry?
notes.back: Streaming SIMD Extensions (SSE) instructions like movaps fault on unaligned stack operands, so the application binary interface (ABI) demands rsp ≡ 0 mod 16 at the call. The pushed return address makes rsp ≡ 8 mod 16 at entry; prologues restore alignment.
notes.extra: Pitfall: hand-written assembly that calls libc with a misaligned stack crashes inside printf on the first movaps.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::04 Code Generation, ABI & Linking
notes.front: What does -fomit-frame-pointer buy and cost?
notes.back: Buys one more general register (rbp) and a shorter prologue. Costs: stack walking must use .eh_frame call frame information (CFI) unwind tables instead of following the rbp chain, which is slower for profilers and impossible for simple in-kernel/eBPF stack walkers.
notes.extra: In practice: distributions have been re-enabling frame pointers (Fedora, Ubuntu) because perf and continuous profilers need cheap unwinding.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::04 Code Generation, ABI & Linking
notes.front: Why does the System V (SysV) application binary interface (ABI) require the caller of a variadic function to set al?
notes.back: al is an upper bound (0–8) on the number of vector registers used for arguments. The callee's prologue saves xmm0–7 into the register save area only when al ≠ 0, so printf without floats skips eight 16-byte stores.
notes.extra: Pitfall: calling printf without a prototype means the compiler may not set al, so %f prints garbage: the classic missing-#include <stdio.h> bug.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::04 Code Generation, ABI & Linking
notes.front: ABI vs API: which changes to a C/C++ library break the ABI while leaving the API intact?
notes.back: Anything that changes the binary contract: struct size or member order, enum underlying size, adding a virtual function or a base class, changing an inline function's body, changing a default argument. Code recompiles fine but old binaries misbehave.
notes.analogy: API is the menu wording; ABI is the shape of the plates. You can keep the menu and still break every dish by changing plate sizes.
notes.extra: In practice: opaque handles plus accessor functions (the pimpl idiom) keep the application binary interface (ABI) stable; abi-compliance-checker/abidiff find breaks.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::04 Code Generation, ABI & Linking
notes.front: Why does C++ mangle names, and what does _Z3addii encode?
notes.back: The linker only knows flat symbol names, but C++ allows overloading, namespaces and templates. _Z marks a mangled name, 3add is the identifier with its length, ii the two int parameters: add(int, int).
notes.extra: In practice: c++filt or nm -C demangles; extern "C" switches it off so C and other languages can link. Rust and Swift mangle too (_R, $s).

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::04 Code Generation, ABI & Linking
notes.front: What does a relocation entry say, and how do R_X86_64_PC32 and R_X86_64_64 differ?
notes.back: “At this offset, patch in this symbol's address plus addend, using this formula.” PC32 stores a 32-bit distance from the instruction (position-independent); _64 stores an absolute 64-bit address and needs fixing at load time if the image moves.
notes.analogy: A form letter with blanks marked “insert address here”; the linker fills the blanks once it knows where everyone lives.
notes.extra: In practice: readelf -r foo.o lists them; the static linker resolves most, the dynamic loader the rest.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::04 Code Generation, ABI & Linking
notes.front: Why is position-independent code nearly free on x86-64 but was costly on 32-bit x86?
notes.back: x86-64 has rip-relative addressing, so code and its own data are reached by a constant offset wherever the image lands. i386 had no PC-relative data addressing: PIC had to compute the global offset table (GOT) address into ebx and lose a register.
notes.extra: Position-independent executable (PIE): the executable itself built as PIC so address space layout randomisation (ASLR) can randomise it; hence the error R_X86_64_32 ... can not be used when making a PIE object; recompile with -fPIE for objects using 32-bit absolute addresses. Link: 06 x86-64 · RIP-relative addressing; 07 ARM64/RISC-V/Z · adrp + add

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::04 Code Generation, ABI & Linking
notes.front: GOT vs PLT: what is each, and why are both needed?
notes.back: Global offset table (GOT): a table of addresses in writable data, filled by the dynamic loader. Procedure linkage table (PLT): tiny code stubs, one per imported function, that jump through the GOT. Code stays read-only and shareable; only the small GOT is patched per process.
notes.analogy: The PLT is a desk of switchboard operators; the GOT is their phone book, updated without rewiring anyone's desk.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::04 Code Generation, ABI & Linking
notes.front: Step through the first call to puts through the procedure linkage table (PLT) with lazy binding.
notes.back: call puts@plt → jmp *GOT[n], which initially points back into the PLT → push the relocation index, jump to PLT[0] → _dl_runtime_resolve finds puts, writes its address into global offset table (GOT)[n], jumps there. Later calls go straight through the GOT.
notes.analogy: Directory enquiries on the first call, speed-dial afterwards.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::04 Code Generation, ABI & Linking
notes.front: Why do hardened builds disable lazy binding with -z now, and what is full RELRO?
notes.back: A lazily bound global offset table (GOT) must stay writable for the process lifetime, so a memory-corruption bug can overwrite a GOT slot and hijack the next library call. -z now resolves everything at load, then relocation read-only (RELRO) remaps the GOT read-only.
notes.extra: Cost: slower startup for programs importing thousands of symbols. checksec reports Partial vs Full RELRO.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::04 Code Generation, ABI & Linking
notes.front: Why does a call from inside libfoo.so to its own exported function foo() still go through the PLT, and why does LD_PRELOAD work at all?
notes.back: Executable and Linkable Format (ELF) symbol interposition: the first definition in load order wins, so the executable or a preloaded library may override foo. The compiler must therefore emit an interposable (PLT) call even to a local definition.
notes.analogy: Company policy says any caller may be redirected by the front desk, so even colleagues in the same office must dial through reception.
notes.extra: In practice: -fvisibility=hidden (export only the real API), -Bsymbolic or protected visibility bind internal calls directly: no PLT, smaller dynamic symbol table, faster dlopen, immune to LD_PRELOAD.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::04 Code Generation, ABI & Linking
notes.front: Static vs dynamic linking: what do you trade?
notes.back: Static: self-contained, fastest startup and calls, link-time optimisation (LTO) over everything; but each binary carries its own libc and a libc security fix means rebuilding all. Dynamic: one shared, patchable copy; but procedure linkage table (PLT) indirection, load-time resolution and version mismatches.
notes.analogy: Every flat with its own boiler versus district heating: independence and no shared outages, or one plant that is cheaper to run and fix for everyone.
notes.extra: In practice: Go and Rust default to static linking of their own code but usually link libc dynamically; container images push many teams back towards fully static (musl).

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::04 Code Generation, ABI & Linking
notes.text: Link-time optimisation (LTO) mechanics: with -flto each .o contains {{c1::compiler IR (LLVM bitcode / GCC GIMPLE bytecode)}} instead of machine code; the linker calls a {{c2::plugin}} that runs the optimiser over the whole program and hands back real objects. {{c3::ThinLTO}} keeps per-module optimisation in parallel, importing only hot functions via a summary index.
notes.extra: Pitfall: full LTO is single-threaded and memory-hungry on big programs; ThinLTO is the practical default (Chrome, Firefox). Link: 03 IR & Optimisation · inlining; devirtualisation

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::04 Code Generation, ABI & Linking
notes.text: Executable and Linkable Format (ELF) thread-local storage (TLS) access models, from fastest to most general: {{c1::local-exec}} (mov %fs:x@tpoff, variable in the executable); {{c2::initial-exec}} (offset loaded from the global offset table (GOT), variable in a library present at startup); {{c3::local-dynamic}} (one __tls_get_addr call for the module, then offsets); {{c4::global-dynamic}} (__tls_get_addr per variable, works after dlopen).
notes.extra: In practice: the compiler picks by -fPIC/-fPIE; -ftls-model=initial-exec speeds up a library you promise never to dlopen.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::04 Code Generation, ABI & Linking
notes.front: A binary built on a new distro fails on an old one with version 'GLIBC_2.34' not found. What mechanism is this?
notes.back: Executable and Linkable Format (ELF) symbol versioning: each glibc symbol carries the version it was introduced or changed in (memcpy@GLIBC_2.14), and the loader refuses to bind if the installed library lacks that version node.
notes.extra: In practice: build on the oldest supported glibc (manylinux containers do exactly this), or link statically.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::04 Code Generation, ABI & Linking
notes.front: How does one libc.so run an Advanced Vector Extensions 2 (AVX2) memcpy on new CPUs and a Streaming SIMD Extensions 2 (SSE2) one on old CPUs?
notes.back: GNU indirect function (IFUNC): the symbol points at a resolver that the dynamic loader runs once (checking cpuid) and whose chosen implementation is written into the global offset table (GOT) slot. All callers are then dispatched at full speed.
notes.extra: Link: 06 x86-64 · SSE/AVX registers; 08 Microarchitecture · branch prediction

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::04 Code Generation, ABI & Linking
notes.text: printf("hi\n") reaches the kernel: Procedure linkage table (PLT) → libc's printf → formatting into the {{c1::FILE buffer of stdout}} → flush (line-buffered on a tty) → {{c2::write(1, buf, n)}} wrapper → the {{c3::syscall}} instruction with the call number in rax → kernel sys_write → tty or pipe driver.
notes.extra: Pitfall: when stdout is a pipe it is fully buffered, so output appears only at exit or when 4 KiB fill: the reason logs “vanish” when a program is killed. Link: 06 x86-64 · syscall convention

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::05 Runtimes: Interpreters, VMs, JIT & GC
notes.front: Why is a bytecode interpreter usually several times faster than a tree-walking interpreter of the same language?
notes.back: Bytecode is a flat, compact array: no pointer-chasing through abstract syntax tree (AST) nodes, no recursive eval() calls per node, and resolved names become slot indices.
notes.analogy: A tree-walker re-reads the recipe book from the index every step; bytecode is the recipe copied onto one card in order.
notes.extra: In practice: Crafting Interpreters' jlox (tree-walking) vs clox (bytecode) differ by well over an order of magnitude on tight loops.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::05 Runtimes: Interpreters, VMs, JIT & GC
notes.front: Stack VM vs register VM: what is the trade-off?
notes.back: Stack VM (Java virtual machine (JVM), CPython, Wasm): tiny instructions, trivial codegen, but more instructions and pushes/pops. Register VM (Lua 5, Dalvik): fewer, larger instructions that name operands directly, so less dispatch overhead.
notes.extra: Example: a = b + c is load b; load c; add; store a on a stack VM, one ADD a, b, c on a register VM.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::05 Runtimes: Interpreters, VMs, JIT & GC
notes.front: Why is threaded code (computed goto at the end of every handler) faster than one big switch in an interpreter loop?
notes.back: A single switch is one indirect jump that must predict every opcode transition; per-handler jumps give the branch predictor a separate history per instruction, so prediction rates rise sharply.
notes.analogy: One receptionist guessing where every visitor goes next, versus each room having its own doorman who knows the usual next stop.
notes.extra: In practice: CPython uses computed gotos (goto *targets[op]) on GCC/Clang. Link: 08 Microarchitecture · branch prediction (indirect branches)

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::05 Runtimes: Interpreters, VMs, JIT & GC
notes.text: CPython executes code as a {{c1::stack-based}} bytecode in the loop in ceval.c; since 3.11 its {{c2::specialising adaptive}} interpreter rewrites hot generic instructions (e.g. BINARY_OP) into type-specialised variants in place ("quickening"), guarded by cheap type checks.
notes.extra: In practice: dis.dis(f, adaptive=True) shows the specialised opcodes. The experimental copy-and-patch just-in-time (JIT) (3.13+) builds on these traces.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::05 Runtimes: Interpreters, VMs, JIT & GC
notes.front: What does CPython's global interpreter lock (GIL) actually protect, and why is removing it hard?
notes.back: It makes the interpreter's shared state, above all non-atomic reference-count updates, safe with one lock. Without it every Py_INCREF needs atomics or biased counting, costing single-thread speed.
notes.extra: In practice: the free-threaded build (PEP 703) is an opt-in alternative interpreter; I/O-bound code already releases the GIL around blocking calls.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::05 Runtimes: Interpreters, VMs, JIT & GC
notes.front: Why do JavaScript engines give objects hidden classes (V8: maps; SpiderMonkey: shapes)?
notes.back: Objects are dictionaries by spec, but most are built the same way. A shared shape maps property name to slot offset, so a property load becomes a shape check plus a fixed-offset load.
notes.analogy: A hotel where every room of a type has the same floor plan: once you know the room type, the bathroom is always the second door.
notes.extra: Mechanism: adding a property moves the object along a transition tree; objects built in the same order share a shape.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::05 Runtimes: Interpreters, VMs, JIT & GC
notes.front: What is an inline cache at a property-access site, and what are its three states?
notes.back: A per-site cache of (shape → offset). Monomorphic: one shape seen; polymorphic: a few (V8: up to 4); megamorphic: too many, so lookups fall back to a global hash table.
notes.extra: Why the just-in-time (JIT) cares: a monomorphic call site names one target, so it can be inlined behind a single shape guard. Link: 08 Microarchitecture · branch prediction (the guard is a branch); 12 Mapping · JS a.b through the IC

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::05 Runtimes: Interpreters, VMs, JIT & GC
notes.front: Why do modern VMs use tiered just-in-time (JIT) compilation instead of one optimising compiler?
notes.back: Optimising compilation is slow and needs profile data that only exists after running. Cheap tiers start fast and collect type feedback; the expensive tier is spent only on code proven hot.
notes.analogy: A newspaper prints a quick wire story first, then sends a reporter to write the deep feature only on stories readers kept clicking.
notes.extra: Trade-off: each tier costs engineering effort and memory for several code versions of the same method. Anchors: V8 runs Ignition (interpreter) → Sparkplug (baseline) → Maglev → TurboFan; HotSpot runs interpreter → C1 → C2.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::05 Runtimes: Interpreters, VMs, JIT & GC
notes.text: HotSpot tiered compilation: level 0 is the {{c1::interpreter}}, levels 1–3 are {{c2::C1}} (3 = with full profiling), level 4 is {{c3::C2}}. The usual path of a hot method is 0 → 3 → 4.
notes.analogy: A three-speed gearbox: start in first, use second while you learn the road, shift to top gear only on a straight you know well.
notes.extra: Why level 2 exists: C1 without heavy profiling is ~30% faster than level 3, so it is used when the C2 queue is backed up. Flag: -XX:+PrintCompilation.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::05 Runtimes: Interpreters, VMs, JIT & GC
notes.front: What does it mean that a just-in-time (JIT) speculates, and what keeps it correct?
notes.back: It compiles for the types and branches seen so far (e.g. "x is always an int") and emits a cheap guard; if the guard fails, execution deoptimises back to a lower tier instead of computing a wrong result.
notes.analogy: A sommelier pours the usual before the order arrives, but keeps the bottle open in case the guest surprises them.
notes.extra: Example: HotSpot's "uncommon trap": a branch never taken during profiling is compiled as a jump to the deoptimiser rather than as real code.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::05 Runtimes: Interpreters, VMs, JIT & GC
notes.front: Mechanically, what happens on deoptimisation?
notes.back: The runtime stops in optimised code, reconstructs the interpreter's frame (locals, operand stack, inlined callers' frames) from a side table, and resumes at the equivalent bytecode; the compiled version is usually thrown away.
notes.extra: Pitfall: a site whose type keeps changing causes deopt/reopt storms; engines eventually give up and leave it generic.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::05 Runtimes: Interpreters, VMs, JIT & GC
notes.front: Speculation in a CPU (08) vs in a just-in-time (JIT) (05): what is the bet, and what is the undo?
notes.back: CPU: predicts branches and addresses, executes ahead, squashes and restarts within tens of cycles, invisibly, per instruction. JIT: assumes the types and call targets seen so far, compiles specialised code behind guards, and on a miss deoptimises in microseconds by rebuilding interpreter frames.
notes.analogy: A sprinter leaning before the gun (cheap to reset) versus a builder who poured foundations on a forecast (expensive to redo).
notes.extra: Same pattern: bet on the past, keep a cheap check and an undo path; both lose when behaviour keeps changing (mispredict storms, deopt storms). Link: 08 Microarchitecture · branch prediction; speculative execution

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::05 Runtimes: Interpreters, VMs, JIT & GC
notes.front: What problem does on-stack replacement (OSR) solve?
notes.back: A long-running loop in a method entered only once would never benefit from tier-up. OSR swaps the live frame into compiled code at a loop back-edge, mid-iteration, mapping interpreter state to the compiled frame.
notes.analogy: Changing a tyre on a moving car: the loop keeps turning while its wheels are swapped for faster ones.
notes.extra: In practice: the same machinery runs in reverse for deopt exits. Benchmarks with one giant main loop measure OSR code, not normal compiled code.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::05 Runtimes: Interpreters, VMs, JIT & GC
notes.front: Just-in-time (JIT) vs ahead-of-time (AOT): what can a JIT do that an AOT compiler cannot, and what does it pay?
notes.back: JIT: sees the real profile and loaded classes, so it can speculate, inline through dynamic dispatch and target the exact CPU. Pays warm-up time, compile CPU, memory for code versions and non-determinism.
notes.extra: In practice: GraalVM Native Image closes the gap at startup by assuming a closed world (reflection must be declared). Link: 03 IR & Optimisation · PGO

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::05 Runtimes: Interpreters, VMs, JIT & GC
notes.front: WebAssembly bytecode vs Java virtual machine (JVM) bytecode: what is the key design difference?
notes.back: Wasm is a low-level target: a typed stack machine over one flat linear memory, no objects, no GC (until the GC proposal), validated in one pass. JVM bytecode is object-level and assumes a garbage-collected heap.
notes.extra: Why: C/C++/Rust need raw memory; bounds-checked linear memory gives a sandbox without trusting the compiler. Structured control flow only (no goto) keeps validation single-pass and streaming.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::05 Runtimes: Interpreters, VMs, JIT & GC
notes.front: Reference counting vs tracing garbage collection (GC): key difference?
notes.back: RC frees an object the moment its count hits zero (prompt, deterministic, work spread evenly) but cannot free cycles and pays a write on every pointer copy. Tracing finds live objects from roots in batches; handles cycles, but pauses and delays reclamation.
notes.extra: Pitfall: a.next = b; b.next = a never reaches zero: CPython adds a cycle collector for exactly this. Java virtual machine (JVM), V8, Go and .NET trace.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::05 Runtimes: Interpreters, VMs, JIT & GC
notes.front: Mark-sweep vs copying collection: what is the trade-off?
notes.back: Mark-sweep touches all live objects then sweeps the whole heap, leaving fragmentation. Copying moves live objects to a fresh space (cost ∝ live data, bump allocation afterwards) but needs double the space and updates every pointer.
notes.extra: In practice: most collectors copy the young generation and mark-sweep (or mark-compact) the old one.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::05 Runtimes: Interpreters, VMs, JIT & GC
notes.front: What is the generational hypothesis, and why does it make garbage collection (GC) cheap?
notes.back: Most objects die young. A small nursery collected often with a copying collector costs only the few survivors; long-lived objects are promoted and scanned rarely.
notes.analogy: Empty the desk inbox daily; sort the filing cabinet once a year.
notes.extra: Example: temporaries, iterators, boxed numbers die within microseconds; caches and sessions live for hours.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::05 Runtimes: Interpreters, VMs, JIT & GC
notes.front: Why does a generational collector need a write barrier and a remembered set / card table?
notes.back: A nursery collection must not scan the whole old generation for roots. The barrier records every store of a young pointer into an old object (marks the card), so only those cards are scanned as extra roots.
notes.analogy: A post-it on the filing cabinet listing which drawers received new inbox items, so the daily inbox clean-up does not re-read every drawer.
notes.extra: In practice: HotSpot's card table marks a 512-byte region per store; the barrier is a couple of instructions per reference store.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::05 Runtimes: Interpreters, VMs, JIT & GC
notes.front: Why can allocation in a garbage collection (GC)'d runtime be faster than malloc?
notes.back: Bump allocation: the thread owns a local buffer (thread-local allocation buffer (TLAB) / nursery) and allocation is "pointer += size" with no locking or free-list search. The cost is paid later, at collection, in proportion to survivors.
notes.extra: Link: 09 Memory · cache lines

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::05 Runtimes: Interpreters, VMs, JIT & GC
notes.text: Tri-colour marking: {{c1::white}} objects are not yet reached (garbage if still white at the end), {{c2::grey}} objects are reached but their children are not yet scanned, {{c3::black}} objects are fully scanned. Marking pops a grey object, greys its white children and blackens it.
notes.extra: Why colours: they let marking be interrupted and resumed, which is what incremental and concurrent collectors need.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::05 Runtimes: Interpreters, VMs, JIT & GC
notes.front: Why does a concurrent marker need a write barrier, in tri-colour terms?
notes.back: The mutator could store a white object into an already-black object and drop the only grey path to it: the object is reachable but never marked. The barrier shades on such stores to keep the invariant "black never points to white".
notes.extra: Invariants: strong = no black→white edge; weak = any black→white edge still has a grey path. Variants: Dijkstra's barrier shades the new target (strong); Yuasa's shades the overwritten value (weak); Go's hybrid barrier does both.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::05 Runtimes: Interpreters, VMs, JIT & GC
notes.front: Incremental vs concurrent garbage collection (GC): key difference?
notes.back: Incremental interleaves small GC steps with the mutator on the same thread (bounded pause, no parallelism). Concurrent runs GC threads alongside mutator threads, so it needs barriers and synchronisation but hides most work.
notes.analogy: Incremental: one cook who tidies between dishes. Concurrent: a second cook tidying while the first keeps cooking, which needs rules about who touches which pan.
notes.extra: In practice: V8 does both (incremental marking plus concurrent marking threads); ZGC and Shenandoah are concurrent including relocation.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::05 Runtimes: Interpreters, VMs, JIT & GC
notes.front: Even with a concurrent collector, where do remaining stop-the-world pauses come from?
notes.back: Root scanning and phase hand-offs: stopping threads at safepoints, scanning stacks and registers, flipping marking state. These scale with thread count and stack depth, not heap size.
notes.extra: In practice: ZGC and Go aim for sub-millisecond pauses by making even relocation concurrent (ZGC: load barriers with coloured pointers).

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::05 Runtimes: Interpreters, VMs, JIT & GC
notes.front: Why does allocation rate often matter more than heap size for garbage collection (GC) overhead?
notes.back: Collection frequency is allocation rate divided by free space; each cycle costs roughly the live set. High allocation with a small heap means scanning the same live data over and over.
notes.analogy: A sink's workload depends on how fast the tap runs, not on how big the basin is.
notes.extra: In practice: giving a service more heap (or GOGC/-Xmx headroom) trades memory for fewer cycles.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::05 Runtimes: Interpreters, VMs, JIT & GC
notes.front: Go's garbage collection (GC) vs HotSpot's generational collectors: what did Go choose differently, and why?
notes.back: Go is non-generational and non-moving: concurrent tri-colour mark-sweep with a hybrid barrier, tuned purely for low pause. It gives up bump allocation and cheap nursery collection, accepting lower throughput for simpler pointers (no relocation, easy cgo).
notes.extra: Link: Go deck · GOGC / GOMEMLIMIT; escape analysis

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::05 Runtimes: Interpreters, VMs, JIT & GC
notes.front: How does Rust's ownership model replace a garbage collector, and what can it not express for free?
notes.back: Every value has one owner; it is freed when the owner goes out of scope, checked at compile time, zero run-time cost and deterministic. Shared or cyclic graphs need Rc/Arc (reference counting) plus Weak, arenas or indices.
notes.extra: Pitfall: Rc cycles leak exactly like CPython without the cycle collector. Link: 02 Types · borrow checker

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::06 ISA & Assembly: x86-64
notes.front: Writing a 32-bit register (eax) zeroes bits 63–32 of rax, but writing ax or al keeps them. Why the asymmetry?
notes.back: Zero-extension on 32-bit writes was a new rule AMD could add in 64-bit mode: it removes a dependency on the old value and lets 32-bit code run "for free". 8/16-bit writes kept the 8086 merge semantics for compatibility.
notes.extra: Consequence: mov al, 1 merges into rax with a false dependency, so compilers prefer movzx. Inventory: 16 general registers (rax…rsp, r8–r15); AArch64's w registers zero-extend the same way. Link: 08 Microarchitecture · register renaming; 07 ARM64/RISC-V/Z · registers

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::06 ISA & Assembly: x86-64
notes.front: Why does every compiler zero a register with xor eax, eax rather than mov rax, 0?
notes.back: Two bytes instead of seven, it zero-extends to 64 bits, and the CPU recognises it as a zeroing idiom with no dependency on the old value of eax.
notes.extra: Pitfall: it clobbers flags; between cmp and jcc the compiler must use mov. Only movabs r64, imm64 takes a 64-bit immediate; all others are sign-extended 32-bit. Link: 08 Microarchitecture · zeroing idiom at rename

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::06 ISA & Assembly: x86-64
notes.text: The arithmetic flags: {{c1::ZF}} (result zero), {{c2::CF}} (unsigned carry/borrow), {{c3::SF}} (sign bit of result), {{c4::OF}} (signed overflow). Most arithmetic logic unit (ALU) instructions set them; mov, lea and cmov leave them untouched.
notes.extra: Also: PF (parity of low byte) and AF (binary-coded decimal (BCD) half-carry) are legacy; inc/dec set everything but CF.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::06 ISA & Assembly: x86-64
notes.front: cmp a, b vs test a, b: what does each compute?
notes.back: cmp performs a - b and discards the result; test performs a & b and discards it. Both only set flags. test eax, eax is the standard "is zero / is negative" check.
notes.extra: Why test: for a zero check it is shorter than cmp eax, 0 and can macro-fuse with the following jcc.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::06 ISA & Assembly: x86-64
notes.front: jl/jg vs jb/ja after a cmp: what is the difference?
notes.back: Less/greater are signed (decided from SF≠OF and ZF); below/above are unsigned (decided from CF and ZF). The same cmp serves both; the jump chooses the interpretation.
notes.analogy: One thermometer reading; whether -1 is "below" 1 depends on whether you read it as a signed or unsigned scale.
notes.extra: Example: cmp eax, -1; ja L is never taken for any eax (0xFFFFFFFF is the largest unsigned value).

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::06 ISA & Assembly: x86-64
notes.text: The general x86-64 memory operand is [base + index*scale + disp], where scale is {{c1::1, 2, 4 or 8}}, base and index are any general register (except rsp as index), and disp is an 8- or 32-bit {{c2::signed}} constant.
notes.extra: Example: mov eax, [rdi + rsi*4 + 16] loads arr->data[i] for 4-byte elements with a 16-byte header, in one instruction.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::06 ISA & Assembly: x86-64
notes.front: Why do compilers use lea for arithmetic, e.g. lea eax, [rdi + rdi*4]?
