notes.back: lea computes the address expression without touching memory: a three-operand add with shift in one cheap instruction, with a free destination register and no flag update. Here it is x*5.
notes.analogy: Using the postcode calculator to do sums: it was built for addresses, but it adds and multiplies by 2/4/8 just fine.
notes.extra: In practice: lea rax,[rdi+rsi] replaces mov rax,rdi; add rax,rsi and keeps flags from an earlier cmp alive.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::06 ISA & Assembly: x86-64
notes.front: What is RIP-relative addressing, and why was it added in x86-64?
notes.back: A memory operand of the form [rip + disp32]. It makes position-independent code cheap: globals and constants are reached by a fixed offset from the current instruction, with no global offset table (GOT) lookup or base-register setup.
notes.analogy: Directions given relative to where you stand ("two doors down") work wherever the building is placed; absolute street numbers do not.
notes.extra: Link: 04 Codegen & ABI · GOT vs PLT

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::06 ISA & Assembly: x86-64
notes.front: AT&T vs Intel syntax: how do you tell them apart and read each?
notes.back: AT&T (GNU default): movl $1, %eax, source first, % registers, $ immediates, size suffix, memory as disp(base,index,scale). Intel: mov eax, 1, destination first, dword ptr [base+index*scale+disp].
notes.extra: In practice: objdump -M intel, gcc -masm=intel; Compiler Explorer defaults to Intel. Mixing them up reverses every operation.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::06 ISA & Assembly: x86-64
notes.front: What exactly do call and ret do on x86-64, and where does the return address live?
notes.back: call pushes the address of the next instruction and jumps; ret pops it into rip. The return address therefore lives in memory on the stack, unlike ARM64's link register.
notes.extra: Pitfall: a push addr; ret trick or an unbalanced call/ret pair confuses the CPU's return-address predictor and costs a string of mispredictions. Link: 08 Microarchitecture · return address stack; 07 ARM64/RISC-V/Z · bl and x30; 04 Codegen & ABI · stack alignment at call

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::06 ISA & Assembly: x86-64
notes.text: x86-64 instruction layout, in order: optional {{c1::legacy prefixes}} (up to 4), optional {{c2::REX}} prefix, {{c3::opcode}} (1–3 bytes), optional {{c4::ModRM}} byte, optional scale-index-base (SIB) byte, optional displacement, optional immediate. Hard maximum: 15 bytes.
notes.extra: Example: 48 8B 44 24 08 = mov rax, [rsp+8]: REX.W, opcode, mode-register-memory (ModRM), SIB, disp8. Prefix magic: F3 0F 10 is movss, F2 0F 10 movsd, 66 0F 10 movupd: same opcode, the prefix picks the instruction; F0 is LOCK.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::06 ISA & Assembly: x86-64
notes.text: The register extension (REX) prefix is 0100WRXB: {{c1::W}} selects 64-bit operand size, {{c2::R}} extends the mode-register-memory (ModRM) reg field, {{c3::X}} extends the scale-index-base (SIB) index, {{c4::B}} extends ModRM rm / SIB base, each adding the fourth bit needed to name r8–r15.
notes.analogy: A fourth digit added to the room-number dial: without it the hotel's new wing (r8–r15) is unreachable.
notes.extra: Side effect: any REX prefix also switches the byte registers from ah/ch/dh/bh to spl/bpl/sil/dil, so the two sets cannot be mixed in one instruction.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::06 ISA & Assembly: x86-64
notes.text: Mode-register-memory (ModRM) is mod(2) reg(3) rm(3): mod = 11 means {{c1::register-to-register}}; other values mean rm is a memory operand with 0-, 8- or 32-bit displacement. rm = 100 means {{c2::a SIB byte follows}} (scale index base), needed for any indexed address or an rsp base.
notes.extra: Quirk: mod=00, rm=101 does not mean [rbp] but [rip+disp32]; that is where RIP-relative addressing lives.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::06 ISA & Assembly: x86-64
notes.front: Why is x86 instruction decoding hard to do in parallel, and how do CPUs cope?
notes.back: Length is unknown until prefixes, opcode and mode-register-memory (ModRM) are parsed, so finding where instruction N+1 starts depends on decoding N. Decoders pre-mark instruction boundaries, speculate lengths at every byte, and cache decoded µops so hot loops skip decode entirely.
notes.analogy: Reading a sentence with no spaces: you can only find the next word once you have finished the current one.
notes.extra: Link: 08 Microarchitecture · µop cache; 07 ARM64/RISC-V/Z · fixed-width encoding

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::06 ISA & Assembly: x86-64
notes.front: Why does an x86-64 CPU still power on in 16-bit real mode and keep decoding 8086 instructions?
notes.back: Binary compatibility is the architecture's commercial moat: every layer (firmware, boot loaders, OS kernels, 30 years of binaries) assumed the old behaviour, so modes were layered on rather than replaced.
notes.extra: In practice: Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (UEFI) firmware switches to 64-bit mode within the first instructions; Intel's X86S proposal (since dropped) explored removing the legacy modes.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::06 ISA & Assembly: x86-64
notes.front: What does rep movsb do, and why does a 2-byte instruction compete with hand-tuned memcpy?
notes.back: It copies rcx bytes from [rsi] to [rdi], direction by direction flag (DF). It is microcoded, so the CPU can choose cache-line-wide moves internally; with ERMSB/FSRM it is fast even for short copies.
notes.extra: Pitfall: older cores had a large start-up cost, so libc switched strategies by size. Link: 08 Microarchitecture · MSROM

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::06 ISA & Assembly: x86-64
notes.text: Single instruction, multiple data (SIMD) register widths: {{c1::xmm}} = 128 bits (SSE), {{c2::ymm}} = 256 bits (AVX), {{c3::zmm}} = 512 bits (AVX-512). Each is the low part of the next; 64-bit mode has 16 of them, AVX-512 raises that to 32.
notes.extra: Example: one vaddps ymm0, ymm1, ymm2 adds 8 floats; zmm does 16. Link: 03 IR & Optimisation · loop vectorisation

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::06 ISA & Assembly: x86-64
notes.front: Why do compilers emit vzeroupper before returning from Advanced Vector Extensions (AVX) code?
notes.back: Legacy Streaming SIMD Extensions (SSE) instructions leave the upper 128 bits of ymm untouched, so after a VEX instruction wrote them the CPU must merge on every SSE op (or pay a state transition). Zeroing the upper halves ends the dirty state.
notes.analogy: Wiping the whiteboard before handing the room to a team that only uses the left half; otherwise they keep working around your leftovers.
notes.extra: Pitfall: calling an SSE-compiled library from AVX code without vzeroupper can cost a large slowdown on older cores.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::06 ISA & Assembly: x86-64
notes.front: What does AVX-512 masking add, and what does k0 mean in an encoding?
notes.back: An opmask register k1–k7 enables per-lane execution: masked-off lanes either keep their old value (merging) or become zero ({z}, zeroing). k0 in the mask field means "no mask" (all lanes).
notes.analogy: A stencil over the vector: paint goes through the holes only; the rest keeps its old colour (merge) or is wiped (zero).
notes.extra: Why: masks turn if inside a loop into predicated lanes and handle loop tails without a scalar remainder. Link: 10 GPU · warp divergence; 07 ARM64/RISC-V/Z · SVE predication

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::06 ISA & Assembly: x86-64
notes.front: What are single instruction, multiple data (SIMD) intrinsics, and when do you reach for them instead of auto-vectorisation?
notes.back: C functions like _mm256_add_ps() (<immintrin.h>) that map roughly one-to-one onto instructions, with the compiler still allocating registers. Use them when the loop shape (shuffles, horizontal ops, saturating math) defeats the vectoriser.
notes.extra: Pitfall: code using Advanced Vector Extensions (AVX) intrinsics needs -mavx2 or __attribute__((target("avx2"))) plus a runtime CPU identification (CPUID) dispatch, or it faults on older CPUs.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::06 ISA & Assembly: x86-64
notes.text: Linux x86-64 syscall convention: number in {{c1::rax}}, arguments in {{c2::rdi, rsi, rdx, r10, r8, r9}}, result in rax (-4095..-1 means -errno); the instruction clobbers {{c3::rcx and r11}}.
notes.extra: Example: mov eax,1; mov edi,1; lea rsi,[rip+msg]; mov edx,len; syscall is write(1, msg, len).

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::06 ISA & Assembly: x86-64
notes.front: The function-call application binary interface (ABI) passes argument 4 in rcx, but the syscall ABI uses r10. Why?
notes.back: The syscall instruction itself overwrites rcx with the return address (and r11 with rflags), so the kernel could never see an argument left there. libc wrappers just mov r10, rcx.
notes.extra: Link: 04 Codegen & ABI · calling conventions; Deep C · SysV register table

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::06 ISA & Assembly: x86-64
notes.front: x86 is little-endian. After mov dword [x], 0x01020304, what does a byte dump of x show, and which instructions reverse it?
notes.back: 04 03 02 01: the least significant byte lives at the lowest address. bswap r32/r64 reverses a register; movbe loads/stores with the swap built in (network byte order).
notes.analogy: Writing a phone number from the last digit: natural once you know, baffling in a hex dump until you do.
notes.extra: In practice: that is why a pointer to a 64-bit value can be read as its low 32 bits at the same address.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::06 ISA & Assembly: x86-64
notes.front: What is the x87 floating-point unit (FPU), and what is it still used for on x86-64?
notes.back: The 1980 coprocessor design: eight 80-bit registers st(0)–st(7) organised as a stack, with extended precision. The x86-64 application binary interface (ABI) moved float/double to Streaming SIMD Extensions (SSE) registers; x87 survives only for long double.
notes.extra: Why it matters: 32-bit x87 code could give different results from 64-bit because intermediates were kept in 80 bits (-ffloat-store, -fexcess-precision).

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::06 ISA & Assembly: x86-64
notes.front: Why did GNU Compiler Collection (GCC) emit rep ret instead of a plain ret for years?
notes.back: AMD K8-era cores could not predict a single-byte ret that was a branch target or followed a conditional jump. The meaningless rep prefix made it two bytes and avoided the penalty; the idiom outlived the hardware.
notes.extra: Lesson: odd code in compiler output usually encodes a microarchitectural workaround; check the date before copying it.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::06 ISA & Assembly: x86-64
notes.front: Why does -O2 compile int f(int x) { return x / 8; } to lea eax,[rdi+7]; test edi,edi; cmovns eax,edi; sar eax,3 rather than a single sar?
notes.back: C integer division truncates toward zero, but an arithmetic shift rounds toward negative infinity. Adding 7 only for negative inputs (branch-free via cmovns) fixes the rounding. Unsigned or known-non-negative x gets the bare shift.
notes.extra: In practice: use unsigned for sizes and indices and the compiler drops the fix-up. Link: 03 IR & Optimisation · strength reduction

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::07 ISA & Assembly: ARM64, RISC-V & IBM Z
notes.text: AArch64 has {{c1::31}} general-purpose 64-bit registers x0–x30; x30 is the {{c2::link register (lr)}}; register number 31 in an encoding means {{c3::sp or xzr (zero register)}} depending on the instruction.
notes.extra: Pitfall: the program counter (PC) is not a general register in AArch64 (it was r15 in 32-bit ARM); you reach it only via adr/adrp and branches.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::07 ISA & Assembly: ARM64, RISC-V & IBM Z
notes.front: What does it mean that AArch64 is a load/store architecture, and why design it that way?
notes.back: Only ldr/str (and pairs/atomics) touch memory; add, and etc. take registers or immediates. Each instruction has at most one, known memory access, which keeps pipelines regular.
notes.analogy: A kitchen where only runners fetch from the pantry and cooks only cook: every job has a predictable shape, so the line never jams.
notes.extra: Contrast: x86 add rax, [rbx] loads and adds in one instruction; the core splits it into two µops anyway. Link: 08 Microarchitecture · micro-fusion

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::07 ISA & Assembly: ARM64, RISC-V & IBM Z
notes.front: Why can't AArch64 load an arbitrary 64-bit constant with a single mov, and what does the compiler emit instead?
notes.back: Every instruction is 32 bits, so only ~16 bits are left for an immediate. A 64-bit constant takes movz plus up to three movk, each writing one 16-bit slice.
notes.analogy: Dictating a 16-digit card number over a line that carries four digits per message: one opener, then three follow-ups that each fill in a slot.
notes.extra: Detail: movz zeroes the register then writes the slice; movk keeps the other bits. Logical ops (and/orr) accept only bitmask immediates (a repeated rotated run of ones, e.g. 0xFF00FF00): a few thousand values in total; anything else must be built in a register first.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::07 ISA & Assembly: ARM64, RISC-V & IBM Z
notes.front: Why does compiled AArch64 code address globals with the pair adrp x0, sym + add x0, x0, :lo12:sym?
notes.back: adrp computes the 4 KiB page of the symbol PC-relatively (±4 GiB reach); add supplies the low 12 bits. Two fixed-size instructions reach any address in a 64-bit program without a literal pool.
notes.extra: Link: 04 Codegen & ABI · relocations; 06 x86-64 · RIP-relative addressing

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::07 ISA & Assembly: ARM64, RISC-V & IBM Z
notes.front: What does csel x0, x1, x2, eq do, and why do compilers love it?
notes.back: Conditional select: x0 = Z ? x1 : x2, using the negative, zero, carry, overflow (NZCV) flags, with no branch. A short if/else that assigns one value becomes branch-free, so it can't mispredict.
notes.extra: Detail: flags are set only by the s-suffixed forms (adds, subs); cmp a, b is an alias of subs xzr, a, b. Link: 08 Microarchitecture · branch prediction; 06 x86-64 · cmov in division fix-up

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::07 ISA & Assembly: ARM64, RISC-V & IBM Z
notes.front: AArch64: how does a call return without a stack, and when must a function save x30?
notes.back: bl f writes the return address into x30 (lr) and jumps; ret jumps to x30. Leaf functions never touch the stack. Any function that itself calls must first save lr, typically stp x29, x30, [sp, #-16]!.
notes.analogy: A single bookmark: fine while you read one book, but open a second and you must put the first bookmark somewhere safe.
notes.extra: Detail: the ! means pre-indexed write-back: sp is decremented first and the new value kept. Link: 04 Codegen & ABI · stack frames; 06 x86-64 · call/ret

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::07 ISA & Assembly: ARM64, RISC-V & IBM Z
notes.front: NEON vs Scalable Vector Extension (SVE): what is the key architectural difference?
notes.back: NEON: 32 fixed 128-bit vectors; the width is baked into the binary. SVE: the implementation picks 128–2048 bits (multiples of 128) and the same binary runs correctly on any width (vector-length agnostic).
notes.extra: In practice: implementations differ: Fujitsu's A64FX ran 512-bit SVE, most Armv9 cores run 128-bit, and the same binary works on both. Link: 03 IR & Optimisation · auto-vectorisation; 06 x86-64 · AVX-512 masking

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::07 ISA & Assembly: ARM64, RISC-V & IBM Z
notes.front: How does a Scalable Vector Extension (SVE) loop process the last partial chunk without a scalar remainder loop?
notes.back: With predicate registers p0–p15: whilelt p0.s, x_i, x_n sets one mask bit per remaining element; predicated loads, ops and stores skip inactive lanes.
notes.analogy: A stencil with some holes taped over: the same brush stroke, but paint only lands where a hole is open.
notes.extra: Why it matters: no peeling or tail code, so the vector loop is the whole loop and code size doesn't grow with vector width.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::07 ISA & Assembly: ARM64, RISC-V & IBM Z
notes.front: ARM64's memory model vs x86-TSO: what extra reordering does ARM allow?
notes.back: Any two independent loads or stores may be reordered (load–load, store–store, load–store), not only a store past a later load as on x86. Ordering must be asked for with ldar/stlr or dmb.
notes.extra: Pitfall: code that is racy but works on x86 breaks on ARM; the bug was always there. Link: 09 Memory · acquire/release mapping; Deep C · barriers x86 vs ARM

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::07 ISA & Assembly: ARM64, RISC-V & IBM Z
notes.front: big.LITTLE / DynamIQ: why mix a few big cores with several little cores that implement the same instruction set architecture (ISA)?
notes.back: The scheduler can migrate a thread between core types transparently; big out-of-order cores take bursts, little in-order cores run background work at a fraction of the energy.
notes.analogy: A hybrid car: the electric motor handles cruising cheaply, the engine kicks in for acceleration, and the driver never changes gear stick.
notes.extra: Pitfall: the cores must expose identical ISA features or a thread migrated mid-flight hits an illegal instruction. Link: 08 Microarchitecture · in-order little cores

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::07 ISA & Assembly: ARM64, RISC-V & IBM Z
notes.text: RISC-V extension letters: I = {{c1::base integer}}, M = {{c2::multiply/divide}}, A = {{c3::atomics}}, F/D = {{c4::single/double float}}, C = {{c5::compressed 16-bit}}, V = {{c6::vectors}}.
notes.extra: Why modular: a microcontroller ships rv32imc, a server rv64gc; the instruction set architecture (ISA) is open, so anyone may implement it and add custom extensions, with vendors competing on microarchitecture rather than on the instruction set. Pitfall: fragmentation, which the RVA profiles (e.g. RVA23) exist to curb.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::07 ISA & Assembly: ARM64, RISC-V & IBM Z
notes.front: What does the instruction set architecture (ISA) string rv64gc mean, and what does the C extension cost the hardware?
notes.back: 64-bit; G = IMAFD + Zicsr + Zifencei (the general-purpose bundle); C adds 16-bit forms of common instructions, cutting code size ~25–30%. Cost: instructions may start on any 2-byte boundary, so fetch must handle two lengths.
notes.extra: Detail: the low two bits of a halfword tell the length (11 = 32-bit), so finding boundaries stays trivial compared with x86. Example: c.add, c.li, c.bnez use the eight most common registers. Link: 06 x86-64 · variable-length decoding

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::07 ISA & Assembly: ARM64, RISC-V & IBM Z
notes.front: Why does RISC-V have no condition-code flags, and what does it do instead?
notes.back: Branches compare two registers directly: beq, bne, blt, bge. No hidden flag register means no implicit dependency between every arithmetic logic unit (ALU) op and the branch, which simplifies out-of-order tracking.
notes.extra: Contrast: x86 and ARM set negative, zero, carry, overflow (NZCV) on cmp and read them in jcc/b.cond; the core must rename the flags like a register. Link: 08 Microarchitecture · register renaming

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::07 ISA & Assembly: ARM64, RISC-V & IBM Z
notes.front: What is a CSR in RISC-V, and how is one read or modified?
notes.back: A control and status register (mstatus, mepc, mcause, mtvec…) in a separate 12-bit address space, accessed with atomic read-modify-write instructions csrrw/csrrs/csrrc.
notes.extra: Example: csrr t0, mcause in a trap handler; csrw mtvec, t0 installs the handler address. The Zicsr extension is what provides these instructions.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::07 ISA & Assembly: ARM64, RISC-V & IBM Z
notes.text: RISC-V privilege levels: {{c1::M (machine)}} is mandatory and highest, running firmware; {{c2::S (supervisor)}} runs the OS; {{c3::U (user)}} runs applications; the {{c4::H (hypervisor)}} extension splits S into HS/VS/VU for virtualisation. ecall traps to the next level up.
notes.extra: In practice: OpenSBI runs in M-mode and Linux in S-mode; tiny MCUs implement M only. Link: 12 Mapping · virtualisation (VMX / SVM / SIE)

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::07 ISA & Assembly: ARM64, RISC-V & IBM Z
notes.front: RISC-V Vector (V) extension: how does a loop learn the vector length, and what family does that put it in?
notes.back: vsetvli t0, a0, e32 asks for a0 32-bit elements and returns the count vl the hardware can do (≤ VLEN/32); the loop strip-mines by vl. Vector-length agnostic, like Scalable Vector Extension (SVE), unlike fixed-width AVX/NEON.
notes.extra: Detail: Vector register length (VLEN) is the implementation's register width (often 128–512 bits); grouping registers (LMUL) lets one instruction act on several. Link: 10 GPU · SIMD vs SIMT

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::07 ISA & Assembly: ARM64, RISC-V & IBM Z
notes.front: Why does z/Architecture still support 24-, 31- and 64-bit addressing modes at once, and why 31 rather than 32?
notes.back: Compatibility: S/360 programs stored flags in the top byte of 24-bit addresses, so extended architecture (XA) could only widen to 31 bits, keeping bit 0 as a mode flag (BASSM). Program status word (PSW) bits select the mode and 1970s binaries still run unchanged.
notes.extra: In practice: SAM24/SAM31/SAM64 switch modes; mixed programs are called trimodal. z/OS itself runs 64-bit while many COBOL applications remain 31-bit (AMODE 31).

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::07 ISA & Assembly: ARM64, RISC-V & IBM Z
notes.text: z/Architecture has {{c1::16}} general registers of 64 bits (plus 16 floating-point, 16 access, 16 control and 32 vector registers); instructions are {{c2::2, 4 or 6}} bytes long, with the length given by the top two bits of the first opcode byte.
notes.extra: Why it matters: length is known before decoding the rest, so despite being complex instruction set computer (CISC), Z decodes far more easily than x86. Big-endian, Extended Binary Coded Decimal Interchange Code (EBCDIC) by convention. Link: 06 x86-64 · variable-length decoding

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::07 ISA & Assembly: ARM64, RISC-V & IBM Z
notes.front: What is a storage-to-storage (SS) instruction on IBM Z, with an example, and why is it the complex instruction set computer (CISC) extreme?
notes.back: Both operands live in memory and the length is in the instruction: MVC 0(80,R6),0(R7) copies 80 bytes in one instruction; AP adds two packed decimals in memory. One instruction does what reduced instruction set computer (RISC) needs a loop for.
notes.extra: Detail: Move characters (MVC)'s length field is 8 bits, so up to 256 bytes; MVCL handles longer moves with registers. Link: 08 Microarchitecture · µop vs microcode

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::07 ISA & Assembly: ARM64, RISC-V & IBM Z
notes.front: How is -1234.56 stored as IBM packed decimal, and why do banks want hardware for it?
notes.back: One digit per nibble, sign in the last nibble (C plus, D minus, F unsigned): 12 34 56 D, four bytes. Decimal arithmetic (AP, SP, MP, ZAP) is exact in base 10, so no binary-float rounding of cents.
notes.analogy: An abacus does money in tens; a binary float is a ruler in inches that can never mark 0.10 exactly.
notes.extra: In practice: COBOL PIC S9(5)V99 COMP-3 maps directly to this; the scale (two decimals) lives in the program, not the data. Newer machines add vector packed-decimal instructions.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::07 ISA & Assembly: ARM64, RISC-V & IBM Z
notes.front: What does the IBM Z SIE instruction do, and who uses it?
notes.back: Start Interpretive Execution: the hypervisor hands the CPU a state description and the guest runs its own privileged code at near-native speed until an interception (I/O, time slice, instruction needing help). PR/SM logical partitions (LPARs) and z/VM both use it, nested two levels deep.
notes.extra: Link: 12 Mapping · virtualisation (VMX / SVM / SIE)

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::07 ISA & Assembly: ARM64, RISC-V & IBM Z
notes.front: IBM Z: a central processor (CP) vs an IBM Z Integrated Information Processor (zIIP): what is the difference, and why does it matter commercially?
notes.back: Same silicon. A zIIP is firmware-restricted to eligible work (Db2 Distributed Relational Database Architecture (DRDA) and utilities, Java, some z/OS services). Time on zIIPs is not counted in the MSU-based software charges, so eligible workloads run cheaper.
notes.analogy: A toll road with a free lane for buses only: same tarmac, but only certain vehicles may use it and it doesn't ring up the meter.
notes.extra: Pitfall: eligible work that spills onto general central processors (CPs) when zIIPs are busy is billed; capacity planning watches that spill.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::07 ISA & Assembly: ARM64, RISC-V & IBM Z
notes.front: Channel I/O on IBM Z: what does the CPU do differently from a Peripheral Component Interconnect Express (PCIe) device driver on x86?
notes.back: The CPU builds a channel program (chain of channel command words (CCWs)) and issues SSCH; the channel subsystem (its own system assist processor (SAP) processors) runs the whole transfer and interrupts once at the end. Almost no CPU cycles go to moving I/O.
notes.analogy: Hand a concierge a full itinerary and go to sleep; the hotel wakes you only when everything is done.
notes.extra: Why it matters: this is a big part of why mainframes handle enormous transaction I/O with modest core counts.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::07 ISA & Assembly: ARM64, RISC-V & IBM Z
notes.front: Which reliability, availability and serviceability (RAS) mechanisms make IBM Z different from commodity servers, not just "more reliable"?
notes.back: Every core checks its own results (duplicated execution/ECC on registers); a faulting instruction is retried transparently; a failing core's state moves to a spare core without the OS noticing; memory uses redundant array of independent memory (RAIM) (RAID-like dual in-line memory module (DIMM) redundancy).
notes.extra: Why it still matters: banking and reservation systems value this plus 60 years of binary compatibility and decimal hardware over raw price/performance.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::07 ISA & Assembly: ARM64, RISC-V & IBM Z
notes.front: Complex instruction set computer (CISC) vs reduced instruction set computer (RISC) today: since both run out-of-order cores on µops, what is the actual dividing line?
notes.back: Encoding regularity and the load/store discipline, not instruction count. RISC: fixed-length, register-to-register, trivial decode. CISC: variable length, memory operands, complex decode that needs µop caches to keep up.
notes.analogy: Printed forms with fixed boxes versus free-text letters: the clerk processes boxes in parallel, but must read each letter to find where the next begins.
notes.extra: Pitfall: "RISC = few instructions" is wrong: AArch64 has well over a thousand encodings. Link: 08 Microarchitecture · µop cache

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::07 ISA & Assembly: ARM64, RISC-V & IBM Z
notes.front: Microcoded vs hardwired decode: how do x86, ARM/RISC-V and IBM Z each handle complex instructions?
notes.back: ARM/RISC-V: nearly everything hardwired into a few µops. x86: hardwired fast path plus a microcode sequencer ROM (MSROM) for the long tail. IBM Z: millicode, a vertical microcode written in z instructions plus privileged extras, for storage-to-storage (SS), decimal and start interpretive execution (SIE) work.
notes.extra: Why: hardwired is fastest; microcode is cheaper to design and patchable. Link: 08 Microarchitecture · MSROM; microcode updates

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::08 Microarchitecture: Pipeline, Out-of-Order & Microcode
notes.front: Instruction set architecture (ISA) vs microarchitecture: what is the difference, and why does it matter for performance claims?
notes.back: The ISA is the contract software sees: registers, instructions, memory model. The microarchitecture is one implementation of it: pipeline depth, caches, out-of-order (OoO) width. Zen and Golden Cove share an ISA but differ in every performance property.
notes.analogy: Sheet music versus a particular orchestra: the notes are fixed, the tempo, section sizes and sound are the orchestra's.
notes.extra: Link: 12 Mapping · hardware/software contract

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::08 Microarchitecture: Pipeline, Out-of-Order & Microcode
notes.front: What does pipelining improve, and what does it not improve?
notes.back: Throughput: with 5 stages, up to one instruction completes per cycle instead of one per 5. Not latency: each instruction still spends 5 stages, and clock speed can rise only because each stage does less.
notes.analogy: Laundry: washer, dryer, folding run on different loads at once; each load still takes the full three steps.
notes.extra: Stages (classic reduced instruction set computer (RISC)): IF fetch, ID decode, EX execute, MEM access, WB write back. Hazards: structural (same unit), data (result not ready), control (next program counter (PC) unknown): fixed by duplication, forwarding and prediction. Superscalar = several pipelines side by side (instructions per cycle (IPC) > 1), orthogonal to pipelining.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::08 Microarchitecture: Pipeline, Out-of-Order & Microcode
notes.front: How does forwarding (bypassing) remove most data-hazard stalls, and which case still stalls?
notes.back: The arithmetic logic unit (ALU) result is routed from the end of EX straight into the next instruction's EX input, instead of waiting for WB. A load-use pair still needs one bubble: loaded data exists only after MEM.
notes.analogy: Passing the dish hand-to-hand down the counter instead of putting it on the shelf and having the next cook fetch it.
notes.extra: In practice: the compiler's scheduler tries to put an independent instruction into that load-use slot. Link: 04 Codegen & ABI · instruction scheduling

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::08 Microarchitecture: Pipeline, Out-of-Order & Microcode
notes.front: Why move from in-order to out-of-order execution? What does an in-order superscalar core do badly?
notes.back: An in-order core stalls everything behind a cache-missing load (head-of-line blocking). OoO lets independent younger instructions execute and later loads start, overlapping several misses: memory-level parallelism.
notes.analogy: A single-queue post office versus one where anyone whose form is complete steps up, while the person waiting on a document stands aside.
notes.extra: Link: 09 Memory · latency numbers

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::08 Microarchitecture: Pipeline, Out-of-Order & Microcode
notes.front: µop vs microcode: what is the difference?
notes.back: A µop is the simple internal operation every decoded instruction becomes (1 for add, 2–3 for push). Microcode is a stored program in the microcode sequencer ROM (MSROM) that generates long µop sequences for complex instructions. Most µops never involve microcode.
notes.analogy: µops are the words; microcode is a phrasebook consulted only for the rare, long expressions.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::08 Microarchitecture: Pipeline, Out-of-Order & Microcode
notes.front: What kinds of things live in the x86 MSROM (microcode ROM)?
notes.back: µop sequences for complex or rare instructions (rep movsb, cpuid, syscall entry, far calls, x87 transcendentals), the sequences that handle faults, interrupts and mode switches, and patchable entry points for updates.
notes.extra: Pitfall: entering the microcode sequencer stalls the normal decoders, so an instruction that needs it costs tens of cycles even when its work is small. Link: 06 x86-64 · rep movsb

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::08 Microarchitecture: Pipeline, Out-of-Order & Microcode
notes.front: Micro-fusion vs macro-fusion on x86 cores: what gets fused, and why bother?
notes.back: Micro-fusion: one instruction's load + ALU (add eax,[rbx]) is one µop in the front end, split only at execution. Macro-fusion: two instructions, cmp/test + jcc, become one µop end to end. Both save front-end and reorder buffer (ROB) slots.
notes.extra: Why: the front end is only 4–6 µops wide, so fusing is free width. In practice: compilers place the cmp immediately before the branch to keep fusion possible. Link: 06 x86-64 · cmp vs test; 11 Accelerators · compiler fusion vs µop fusion

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::08 Microarchitecture: Pipeline, Out-of-Order & Microcode
notes.front: Why do x86 cores have a decoded µop cache (Intel's decoded stream buffer (DSB)), and what does it change about the variable-length cost?
notes.back: It caches already decoded µops keyed by fetch address. Hot loops are fed from it, bypassing the length decoders entirely (less power, shorter pipeline). x86 pays the variable-length tax mainly on cold code.
notes.extra: Link: 07 ARM64/RISC-V/Z · fixed 32-bit encoding

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::08 Microarchitecture: Pipeline, Out-of-Order & Microcode
notes.front: How does a microcode update actually get applied to a CPU?
notes.back: BIOS or the OS writes the update's memory address to a model-specific register (Intel: WRMSR 0x79); the CPU verifies the vendor's signature, loads the patch into on-chip patch RAM, and match registers redirect microcode sequencer ROM (MSROM) entry points to it. Volatile: redone every boot.
notes.analogy: Sticky notes over specific pages of a reference book, reapplied every morning because the cleaner removes them overnight.
notes.extra: In practice: Linux loads it from the initrd very early; late loading on a running system is discouraged because MSRs can vanish mid-update.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::08 Microarchitecture: Pipeline, Out-of-Order & Microcode
notes.front: Why must microcode updates be signed, and what can they fix versus not fix?
notes.back: Unsigned, an attacker could rewrite instruction semantics below the OS. They can change anything that passes through microcode or has a hook: add flushes, disable features, insert mitigations (Spectre v2 indirect branch restricted speculation (IBRS)). They cannot fix a hardwired datapath such as a wrong adder.
notes.extra: Example: the Pentium FDIV bug was a hardwired table, fixed only by replacing chips; many Spectre-class mitigations shipped as microcode.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::08 Microarchitecture: Pipeline, Out-of-Order & Microcode
notes.front: Register renaming: what problem does it solve, and how?
notes.back: False dependencies (write-after-read (WAR), write-after-write (WAW)): with 16–32 architectural names, reuse would serialise independent work. Each write gets a fresh physical register from a file of hundreds; only true read-after-write (RAW) dependencies remain to order execution.
notes.analogy: A whiteboard with 16 labelled spots versus a fresh index card for every result: the label just points at the newest card.
notes.extra: Detail: the map (RAT) is checkpointed so a flush can restore it. Link: 04 Codegen & ABI · register allocation vs renaming; 07 ARM64/RISC-V/Z · RISC-V has no flags

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::08 Microarchitecture: Pipeline, Out-of-Order & Microcode
notes.front: Why does xor eax, eax cost no execution-unit cycle on modern x86?
notes.back: The renamer recognises the zeroing idiom and points eax at a known-zero physical register with no dependency on the old value. Register-to-register mov is likewise often eliminated at rename.
notes.extra: Link: 06 x86-64 · xor eax,eax idiom

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::08 Microarchitecture: Pipeline, Out-of-Order & Microcode
notes.front: What does the scheduler (reservation stations) do every cycle in an out-of-order core?
notes.back: Holds µops waiting for operands; when a producing µop finishes it wakes up consumers by tag; among ready µops the select logic picks the oldest per execution port and issues it.
notes.extra: Pitfall: scheduler size, not reorder buffer (ROB) size, often limits how far ahead a core can look past a long dependency chain.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::08 Microarchitecture: Pipeline, Out-of-Order & Microcode
notes.front: What is the reorder buffer (ROB) for, and why retire in order when we executed out of order?
notes.back: It holds every in-flight µop in program order; results commit only at the head. The architectural state is always a prefix of the program, so exceptions are precise and a mispredict is undone by discarding everything younger.
notes.analogy: A numbered conveyor: items are worked on in any order, but leave the factory strictly by ticket number.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::08 Microarchitecture: Pipeline, Out-of-Order & Microcode
notes.text: Branch prediction hardware: the {{c1::direction predictor}} guesses taken or not; the {{c2::BTB (branch target buffer)}} remembers where a branch went last time; the {{c3::return address stack}} predicts ret targets by mirroring calls and returns.
notes.extra: Link: Cloud Architecture · cost of a branch mispredict

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::08 Microarchitecture: Pipeline, Out-of-Order & Microcode
notes.front: Tagged geometric history length (TAGE): what is the core idea behind the branch predictors in modern high-end cores?
notes.back: Several tables indexed by a hash of the program counter (PC) and global branch history of geometrically increasing lengths, each entry partially tagged. The longest-history table that hits provides the prediction. Long patterns are captured while most storage serves short histories.
notes.analogy: Ask every witness; trust the one with the longest relevant memory who actually recognises this situation.
notes.extra: In practice: TAGE-SC-L variants (plus statistical corrector and loop predictor) win the branch-prediction championships and resemble shipping designs.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::08 Microarchitecture: Pipeline, Out-of-Order & Microcode
notes.front: Why does a ret need its own predictor (return address stack) rather than the BTB?
notes.back: One ret has many targets, one per call site, so a BTB entry keyed by its address is always stale. The RAS pushes on call and pops on ret, mirroring the stack in hardware.
notes.extra: Pitfall: very deep recursion overflows the RAS (tens of entries), after which returns mispredict. Retpolines deliberately exploit RAS prediction to defeat Spectre v2.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::08 Microarchitecture: Pipeline, Out-of-Order & Microcode
notes.front: What is the store buffer, and what does it make visible to other cores?
notes.back: Retired stores park there and drain to cache later, so a store need not wait the ~100 cycles to own the line. The core's own loads check it (store-to-load forwarding); other cores cannot see it yet. That gap is the store→load reordering even x86-TSO allows.
notes.analogy: An outbox: you keep working while letters wait for the post, but colleagues cannot read a letter still in your outbox.
notes.extra: Link: 09 Memory · TSO & the store-buffering litmus test; Deep C · smp_mb()

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::08 Microarchitecture: Pipeline, Out-of-Order & Microcode
notes.front: Memory disambiguation: what is the problem, and how do cores solve it?
notes.back: A load may be younger than a store whose address is still unknown, so it can't be sure they don't alias. A predictor guesses no alias and lets the load run early; if the store's address later matches, the pipeline is cleared and re-executed.
notes.extra: Pitfall: the speculative window where the load read stale data is Spectre v4 (speculative store bypass).

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::08 Microarchitecture: Pipeline, Out-of-Order & Microcode
notes.front: Spectre v1 (bounds-check bypass): walk through the mechanism.
notes.back: Train if (i < len) to predict taken; then pass a huge i. The core speculatively reads a[i] (a secret) and uses it as an index into b[], pulling that line into cache. The work is squashed, but timing b[] reveals the secret byte.
notes.extra: Mitigations: lfence after the check, or index masking so the speculative access cannot leave bounds. Link: 12 Mapping · Spectre as a contract breach

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::08 Microarchitecture: Pipeline, Out-of-Order & Microcode
notes.front: Spectre v2 vs Meltdown: how do their hardware mechanisms differ?
notes.back: v2: attacker trains the BTB so the victim's indirect branch speculatively jumps to a gadget (branch target injection). Meltdown: a load of kernel memory is permission-checked only at retirement, after dependents already used the value. Predictor abuse versus a deferred fault.
notes.extra: Fixes: retpoline / indirect branch restricted speculation (IBRS) for v2, kernel page-table isolation (KPTI) for Meltdown. Why fundamental: speculation is architecturally invisible but microarchitecturally visible (caches, predictors, port contention), so any shared state touched on a squashed path is a potential side channel.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::08 Microarchitecture: Pipeline, Out-of-Order & Microcode
notes.front: SMT (hyper-threading): why does it raise throughput on an out-of-order core, and when does it hurt?
notes.back: Issue slots sit idle while one thread waits on a miss or mispredict; a second thread with its own registers and rename map fills them. It hurts when both threads are compute-bound and fight for the same ports, caches and translation lookaside buffer (TLB): each runs slower.
notes.analogy: Two cooks sharing one stove: when one waits for water to boil, the other uses the burners.
notes.extra: Pitfall: shared caches and ports leak timing between tenants, which is why some clouds disable SMT or pin sibling threads to one VM.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::08 Microarchitecture: Pipeline, Out-of-Order & Microcode
notes.text: Top-Down analysis sorts each pipeline slot per cycle into {{c1::Retiring}} (useful work), {{c2::Bad Speculation}} (work later flushed), {{c3::Front-End Bound}} (no µops delivered) or {{c4::Back-End Bound}} (µops waiting for memory or execution resources).
notes.extra: In practice: perf stat --topdown or VTune starts here; most server code is back-end (memory) bound, and only then do you drill into cache misses. Link: 12 Mapping · which layer to blame

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::08 Microarchitecture: Pipeline, Out-of-Order & Microcode
notes.front: A reduction loop for (...) sum += a[i]; runs far below the core's width. What limits it, and what does the compiler do?
notes.back: The loop-carried dependency through sum: each add waits for the previous one, so instructions per cycle (IPC) is bounded by 1/latency of the add (about 4 cycles for FP). The compiler unrolls with several independent accumulators to expose parallelism.
notes.extra: Pitfall: for floating point that reassociation changes rounding, so the compiler may only do it under -ffast-math / -fassociative-math. Link: 03 IR & Optimisation · FP reductions & -ffast-math; 12 Mapping · the loop through every layer

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::08 Microarchitecture: Pipeline, Out-of-Order & Microcode
notes.front: Apple's M-series cores vs typical x86 cores: what is the structural reason for their high IPC at lower clocks?
notes.back: Fixed-length AArch64 lets them decode 8+ instructions per cycle cheaply and feed a very deep out-of-order window (reorder buffer (ROB) of many hundreds) with many execution units. x86 reaches similar width only via the µop cache and fusion tricks, and at higher clocks.
notes.extra: Link: 07 ARM64/RISC-V/Z · fixed-width encoding

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::08 Microarchitecture: Pipeline, Out-of-Order & Microcode
notes.front: Why are Arm's "little" cores in-order, when out-of-order is clearly faster?
notes.back: Renaming, reorder buffer (ROB), schedulers and recovery logic burn area and power on every cycle whether or not they find parallelism. For background work, a 2–3 wide in-order core with good caches gives acceptable speed at a fraction of the energy.
notes.extra: Link: 07 ARM64/RISC-V/Z · big.LITTLE; 10 GPU · latency hiding across warps

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::09 Memory Hierarchy, Caches & Coherence
notes.text: Orders of magnitude on a modern server core: L1 hit {{c1::~1 ns (a few cycles)}}, L3 hit {{c2::~10 ns}}, dynamic RAM (DRAM) {{c3::~100 ns}}, Non-Volatile Memory Express (NVMe) read {{c4::~100 µs}}, which is why one cache miss costs about as much as a few hundred simple instructions.
notes.analogy: L1 is the desk, L3 the bookshelf in the room, DRAM the library across the street, NVMe a parcel from another city.
notes.extra: In practice: numbers drift with each chip; the ratios (×10 per level, ×1000 to storage) are what to remember.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::09 Memory Hierarchy, Caches & Coherence
notes.front: Why do caches move whole 64-byte lines instead of the single word a load asks for?
notes.back: Spatial locality: the neighbours are likely needed next, and one tag plus one transfer is amortised over 64 bytes.
notes.analogy: A librarian fetching one book brings the whole shelf, betting you will want the books beside it.
notes.extra: Pitfall: the bet fails for strided or random access: you pay for 64 bytes and use 4. Link: 12 Mapping · a[i]+=b[i] through cache lines

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::09 Memory Hierarchy, Caches & Coherence
notes.front: How is a 64-bit address split to look up a set-associative cache?
notes.back: Low bits: offset within the line (6 bits for 64 B). Next bits: index selecting the set. Remaining high bits: tag, compared against every way of that set in parallel.
notes.extra: Example: 32 KB, 8-way, 64 B lines → 64 sets → 6 index bits (bits 11..6).

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::09 Memory Hierarchy, Caches & Coherence
notes.front: What does higher associativity buy, and what does it cost?
notes.back: Buys fewer conflict misses (several hot lines can map to the same set). Costs more tag comparators, more energy per lookup and a slightly longer hit path.
notes.analogy: A coat check with 8 hooks per ticket number instead of 1: fewer fights over a hook, but more hooks to scan.
notes.extra: In practice: L1 is 8–12-way, L2/L3 up to 16-way or more; direct-mapped caches are rare today outside tiny embedded cores.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::09 Memory Hierarchy, Caches & Coherence
notes.front: Why do L1 data caches index with the virtual address but tag with the physical one (VIPT)?
notes.back: The set can be selected before address translation finishes, so the translation lookaside buffer (TLB) lookup and the cache lookup run in parallel; the physical tag then confirms the hit with no aliasing problems.
notes.analogy: Walking to the right aisle from the first digits of a call number while the catalogue still resolves the rest.
notes.extra: Link: 08 Microarchitecture · forwarding & load-use latency

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::09 Memory Hierarchy, Caches & Coherence
notes.front: Why is an L1 data cache typically 32 KB 8-way or 48 KB 12-way, rather than, say, 64 KB 4-way?
notes.back: Virtually indexed, physically tagged (VIPT) only works if the index bits lie inside the page offset, i.e. way size ≤ page size (4 KB). More capacity therefore has to come from more ways, not more sets.
notes.extra: What breaks: a 16 KB way would let one physical line live in two sets (a synonym), needing extra hardware to find and invalidate the twin.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::09 Memory Hierarchy, Caches & Coherence
notes.front: Why do L2/L3 caches not use true least recently used (LRU) replacement?
notes.back: Tracking exact recency across 16 ways is costly, and LRU is defeated by streaming scans that evict the whole useful working set. They use tree-PLRU or RRIP-style policies that resist scans.
notes.analogy: A bouncer who admits newcomers only to a probation spot near the exit: one pass through the club doesn't throw out the regulars.
notes.extra: In practice: Intel's adaptive policies and AMD's re-reference interval prediction (RRIP) variants insert new lines with low priority unless they prove reuse.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::09 Memory Hierarchy, Caches & Coherence
notes.front: Why does writing one byte to a line not in cache trigger a read from memory first?
notes.back: Write-allocate: the cache must own the whole 64 B line before merging the byte, so it issues a read-for-ownership (RFO). A plain memset of a huge buffer therefore reads as much as it writes.
notes.extra: Policies: write-back marks the line dirty and writes memory only on eviction; write-through forwards every store (simpler, more traffic). CPU data caches are write-back. In practice: non-temporal stores (movntdq) and rep stosb fast paths skip the RFO and stream to memory.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::09 Memory Hierarchy, Caches & Coherence
notes.front: Inclusive vs exclusive cache hierarchy: what does each buy?
notes.back: Inclusive (L3 holds everything L1/L2 hold): L3 can act as a snoop filter, no need to probe cores. Exclusive/victim (lines live in one level only): more usable capacity.
notes.extra: Example: Intel's older ring-bus parts were inclusive; AMD Zen's L3 is a victim cache filled by L2 evictions, so L2 + L3 capacity adds up. Non-inclusive non-exclusive (NINE) sits in between.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::09 Memory Hierarchy, Caches & Coherence
notes.text: Cache roles: {{c1::L1}} is split into instruction and data caches, private, tuned for latency; {{c2::L2}} is private and unified, hiding L1 misses; {{c3::L3 (LLC)}} is shared by the cores, sliced per core and reached over a ring or mesh.
notes.extra: Why it matters: an L3 hit costs ~40 cycles partly because the line may sit in another core's slice across the interconnect.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::09 Memory Hierarchy, Caches & Coherence
notes.front: Why does a linked-list traversal defeat the hardware prefetcher, while an array scan does not?
notes.back: Prefetchers predict addresses from patterns (next line, constant stride). In a list each address is only known after the previous load returns, so every node is a full memory latency.
notes.analogy: A treasure hunt where each clue is inside the previous box: nobody can run ahead to open the next one.
notes.extra: In practice: a software prefetch (__builtin_prefetch) helps only when the address is computable far ahead, e.g. a[idx[i+16]]. Link: 10 GPU · pointer chasing

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::09 Memory Hierarchy, Caches & Coherence
notes.text: Modified-Exclusive-Shared-Invalid (MESI) line states: {{c1::Modified}} = dirty and the only copy; {{c2::Exclusive}} = clean and the only copy; {{c3::Shared}} = clean, other caches may hold it; {{c4::Invalid}} = no valid data.
notes.extra: Why E exists: read-then-write of private data is the common case; from E the write becomes M silently, from S it would need an invalidation broadcast every time.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::09 Memory Hierarchy, Caches & Coherence
notes.front: Core A writes a line that core B holds in Shared state. What happens under Modified-Exclusive-Shared-Invalid (MESI)?
notes.back: A sends an invalidation (upgrade/RFO); B's copy becomes Invalid; A's becomes Modified. When B reads again, A must write the line back and both drop to Shared.
notes.analogy: One shared whiteboard marker: to write, you grab it and everyone else's photo of the board is declared stale.
notes.extra: Pitfall: two cores alternately writing the same line ping-pong it at ~100 cycles a bounce; this is the mechanism behind false sharing.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::09 Memory Hierarchy, Caches & Coherence
notes.front: Modified-Owned-Exclusive-Shared-Invalid (MOESI)'s Owned and Modified-Exclusive-Shared-Invalid-Forward (MESIF)'s Forward state: what problem do they solve?
notes.back: Who answers a snoop for a line in several caches. Owned (AMD): a dirty line can be shared without writing it back; the owner supplies it. Forward (Intel): one clean sharer is designated to respond, so memory and others stay quiet.
notes.extra: Why it matters: both cut memory traffic when data is widely read; the protocol name tells you which vendor's manual to open.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::09 Memory Hierarchy, Caches & Coherence
notes.front: Coherence vs memory consistency: key difference?
notes.back: Coherence: all cores eventually agree on the value sequence of one location (Modified-Exclusive-Shared-Invalid (MESI) gives this). Consistency: the rules for the order in which accesses to different locations become visible (SC, total store order (TSO), weak).
notes.analogy: Coherence: everyone eventually reads the same version of each page. Consistency: whether everyone sees the pages updated in the same order.
notes.extra: Pitfall: a perfectly coherent x86 still lets a later load pass an earlier store; coherence alone never makes a lock correct.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::09 Memory Hierarchy, Caches & Coherence
notes.text: Memory models: {{c1::sequential consistency}} = one global interleaving in program order; {{c2::TSO (x86, SPARC)}} = only a store may be delayed past a later load (store buffer); {{c3::weak / relaxed (ARM, POWER, RISC-V)}} = loads and stores may reorder freely unless fenced.
notes.extra: Link: 07 ARM64/RISC-V/Z · weak ordering; Deep C · barriers x86 vs ARM

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::09 Memory Hierarchy, Caches & Coherence
notes.front: Thread 1: x=1; r1=y. Thread 2: y=1; r2=x. Can both r1 and r2 be 0 on x86?
notes.back: Yes. Each store waits in its core's store buffer while the following load reads memory, so both loads can run before either store is visible. Only mfence or a lock-ed instruction between them forbids it.
notes.extra: Why it matters: this is the store-buffering (SB) litmus test; Dekker/Peterson locks are broken on total store order (TSO) without a fence.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::09 Memory Hierarchy, Caches & Coherence
notes.front: How do acquire loads and release stores map to instructions on x86 vs ARM64?
notes.back: x86: plain mov for both (total store order (TSO) already gives the ordering); only a seq_cst store needs xchg or mfence. ARM64: dedicated ldar / stlr; plain ldr/str would be reordered.
notes.extra: Why it matters: relaxed and acquire/release atomics are nearly free on x86, so 'atomics are slow' is really about seq_cst and contention. Link: 07 ARM64/RISC-V/Z · ARM vs TSO

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::09 Memory Hierarchy, Caches & Coherence
notes.front: How does lock cmpxchg make a read-modify-write atomic on a modern x86?
notes.back: The core takes the line in Modified state and holds it (cache lock) for the duration, so no other core can intervene; no bus-wide lock is needed unless the operand straddles two lines.
notes.extra: Pitfall: a split lock (operand crossing a cache line) falls back to a system-wide bus lock costing ~1000 cycles for everyone; Linux can detect and kill offenders (split_lock_detect).

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::09 Memory Hierarchy, Caches & Coherence
notes.front: LL/SC (ARM ldxr/stxr, RISC-V lr/sc) vs CAS (x86 cmpxchg): key difference?
notes.back: CAS compares a value, so it misses an A→B→A change (ABA). LL/SC tracks the address with a reservation and the store fails if anyone wrote in between, but it can fail spuriously, so it always loops.
notes.extra: In practice: ARMv8.1 Large System Extensions (LSE) added single-instruction atomics (cas, ldadd) because LL/SC loops scale poorly under contention.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::09 Memory Hierarchy, Caches & Coherence
notes.front: How do you find false sharing in a running program on Linux?
notes.back: perf c2c record then perf c2c report: it lists cache lines with HITM (hit in another core's Modified line) and the offsets within the line each thread touched.
notes.extra: Example: a read-mostly config field beside a hot per-thread counter in one struct. Link: Deep C · false sharing & kernel remedies

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::09 Memory Hierarchy, Caches & Coherence
notes.front: What is translation lookaside buffer (TLB) reach, and why do huge pages help even when the page walk itself is cheap?
notes.back: Reach = entries × page size, e.g. ~1500 × 4 KB ≈ 6 MB, far below a server's working set. 2 MB pages multiply the reach ×512 so most translations never miss at all.
notes.extra: In practice: this is the capacity argument for transparent huge pages and 1 GB pages in databases and Data Plane Development Kit (DPDK). Link: Linux Internals · TLB & huge pages

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::09 Memory Hierarchy, Caches & Coherence
notes.front: A 4-level page walk could cost four memory accesses. Why is a translation lookaside buffer (TLB) miss usually much cheaper?
notes.back: Page-table entries are ordinary cacheable data, so the walker usually hits L1/L2, and paging-structure caches keep the upper levels, leaving one or two real accesses.
notes.analogy: Looking up an address in a 4-volume atlas where the first three volumes are already open on the desk.
notes.extra: Pitfall: under virtualisation the nested walk is 2-D (up to 24 lookups), which is why huge pages matter even more for VMs.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::09 Memory Hierarchy, Caches & Coherence
notes.front: Dynamic RAM (DRAM): why is an access to the bank's already-open row much faster than one to another row?
notes.back: A row-buffer hit is just a column read. A miss needs precharge (close the old row) then activate (sense the new row into the buffer) before the column read: roughly three times the latency.
notes.analogy: A filing cabinet: pulling another sheet from the open drawer is quick; opening a different drawer means closing this one first.
notes.extra: Organisation: channel → rank → banks (independent) → rows → columns; each bank has one row buffer. Controllers interleave consecutive lines across banks and channels so sequential streams hit open rows in parallel.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::09 Memory Hierarchy, Caches & Coherence
notes.front: Bandwidth vs latency: why does doubling memory bandwidth not speed up a pointer-chasing loop?
notes.back: Latency is the time for one dependent access; bandwidth is how many can be in flight. Pointer chasing issues one at a time, so it is bounded by latency (~100 ns) however wide the pipe.
notes.analogy: A wider motorway does not shorten a single car's trip; it only lets more cars travel at once.
notes.extra: Little's law: achieved bandwidth = outstanding requests ÷ latency, so saturating dynamic RAM (DRAM) needs tens of misses in flight (line-fill buffers, prefetch, many cores).

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::09 Memory Hierarchy, Caches & Coherence
notes.front: What does the Roofline model tell you about a kernel?
notes.back: Plot attainable floating-point operations per second (FLOP/s) against arithmetic intensity (floating-point operations (FLOPs) per byte moved). Below the ridge point the kernel is memory-bound and only less traffic helps; above it, compute-bound and only better instructions help.
notes.extra: Example: a dot product does ~1 floating-point operation (FLOP) per 8 bytes: hopelessly memory-bound; a large matmul reuses each byte hundreds of times. Link: 11 Accelerators · ridge point; 12 Mapping · performance models

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::10 GPU Architecture & Programming Model
notes.front: Single instruction, multiple data (SIMD) vs single instruction, multiple threads (SIMT): key difference?
notes.back: SIMD: one thread issues one wide instruction over a vector register; lanes are explicit in the code. SIMT: each lane is written as an independent scalar thread; hardware groups 32 into a warp that shares one instruction stream.
notes.analogy: SIMD is one chef chopping 8 carrots with a wide blade; SIMT is 32 cooks reading the same recipe line aloud, each on their own carrot.
notes.extra: Why it matters: SIMT hides the vector width and allows per-thread branching (at a divergence cost); SIMD exposes it and needs masks written by hand. Link: 06 x86-64 · AVX; 07 ARM64/RISC-V/Z · SVE / RVV

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::10 GPU Architecture & Programming Model
notes.text: CUDA launch hierarchy: a kernel runs as a {{c1::grid}} of {{c2::thread blocks}}; each block runs entirely on one {{c3::SM}}, and its threads are executed 32 at a time as {{c4::warps}}.
notes.extra: Link: Cloud Architecture · warp & SM definitions

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::10 GPU Architecture & Programming Model
notes.front: Why must a thread block run entirely on one streaming multiprocessor (SM)?
notes.back: Its threads share that SM's shared memory and synchronise with __syncthreads(), a hardware barrier that only exists inside an SM.
notes.extra: Consequence: blocks are the unit of scheduling, dispatched in any order as streaming multiprocessors (SMs) free up; a block must never wait for another block (deadlock), so inter-block sync needs atomics or a cooperative grid launch.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::10 GPU Architecture & Programming Model
notes.front: How does a GPU hide a ~500-cycle global memory latency without out-of-order execution or large caches?
notes.back: Each streaming multiprocessor (SM) keeps many warps resident with all their registers; every cycle the warp schedulers issue from whichever warps are ready. A stalled warp costs nothing; another warp fills the slot.
notes.analogy: A dentist with ten chairs: while one patient's anaesthetic sets, the dentist works on the others; no chair is ever cleared and re-set.
notes.extra: Contrast: a CPU hides latency within one thread (OoO, prediction); a GPU hides it across threads (TLP). Link: 08 Microarchitecture · out-of-order execution

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::10 GPU Architecture & Programming Model
notes.front: What is occupancy on a streaming multiprocessor (SM)?
notes.back: Resident warps divided by the maximum the SM can hold (e.g. 64 warps). It is limited by registers per thread, shared memory per block and the block-count cap.
notes.extra: In practice: nvcc -Xptxas -v prints registers and shared memory per kernel; Nsight Compute shows achieved occupancy and which resource limits it.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::10 GPU Architecture & Programming Model
notes.front: Why is 100% occupancy not always the goal?
notes.back: Latency only has to be covered: a few warps each with lots of independent work (instruction-level parallelism (ILP), several loads in flight) can saturate the units at low occupancy, while using the saved registers for bigger tiles.
notes.extra: Example: tuned general matrix multiply (GEMM) kernels run at 25–50% occupancy with huge register tiles; naive kernels need high occupancy because each warp issues one load then waits.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::10 GPU Architecture & Programming Model
notes.front: What is shared memory on a streaming multiprocessor (SM), and why is it faster than hitting L1?
notes.back: A programmer-managed scratchpad per block (tens to ~200 KB per SM, carved from the same static RAM (SRAM) as L1). You decide what to stage, so there are no tags, no misses, and data is reused by all threads in the block.
notes.analogy: A whiteboard in the team room: everyone in the block writes and reads it, nobody outside can see it.
notes.extra: Example: tiled matmul loads a tile once into shared memory and reuses it across threads. Link: 11 Accelerators · compiler-driven tiling

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::10 GPU Architecture & Programming Model
notes.front: Why can a stride-2 access to shared memory run at half speed?
notes.back: Shared memory has 32 banks, each 4 bytes wide; threads hitting different addresses in the same bank serialise. Stride 2 maps 32 threads onto 16 banks: a 2-way bank conflict.
notes.extra: Fix: pad arrays (tile[32][33]) or swizzle indices; broadcast (all threads, same address) is conflict-free.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::10 GPU Architecture & Programming Model
notes.front: What does the hardware do with if (threadIdx.x % 2) A(); else B(); inside a warp?
notes.back: Both paths execute: A with odd lanes masked off, then B with even lanes masked off. The warp takes the time of both branches and only half the lanes do useful work.
notes.analogy: A tour group where half want the museum and half the park: the bus visits both, each half waiting on the bus while the others look.
notes.extra: Fix: make the condition depend on threadIdx.x / 32 so whole warps take the same path; divergence inside a warp is what costs, not branches per se.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::10 GPU Architecture & Programming Model
notes.front: What changed with Volta's independent thread scheduling, and why do warp intrinsics now end in _sync?
notes.back: Each thread got its own program counter and call stack, so lanes of a diverged warp may interleave instead of strictly running one side to completion. Code must therefore say which lanes participate: the mask argument of __shfl_sync, __ballot_sync.
notes.extra: Pitfall: pre-Volta code that assumed lockstep reconvergence can deadlock or read stale lanes; __syncwarp() restores an explicit warp barrier.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::10 GPU Architecture & Programming Model
notes.front: What makes a warp's global memory access coalesced?
notes.back: Hardware merges the 32 addresses into aligned 32-byte sectors; each touched sector is one transaction. Consecutive threads reading consecutive 4-byte words, aligned, touch 4 sectors for 128 bytes: 100% efficiency.
notes.extra: Pitfall: stride-4 floats touch 16 sectors for the same 128 useful bytes: 25% efficiency; random access approaches 1 sector per thread. Link: 09 Memory · cache lines; 10 GPU · cache line vs sector

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::10 GPU Architecture & Programming Model
notes.front: CPU cache line (09) vs GPU coalescing sector (10): same idea?
notes.back: Both are the unit memory moves in, and both punish strides. A cache line (64 B, one tag) serves one thread's locality over time. A sector (32 B) is formed from the addresses of 32 threads at one instant: locality across the warp, not across time.
notes.analogy: A season ticket for one regular commuter versus a minibus that picks up whoever is standing in a row right now.
notes.extra: Lesson: on a CPU keep what one thread needs together (array of structures (AoS) can be fine); on a GPU keep what neighbouring threads need together (SoA). Link: 09 Memory · cache lines; 10 GPU · AoS vs SoA

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::10 GPU Architecture & Programming Model
notes.front: Why does an array of structs (AoS) hurt a GPU kernel that reads one field per thread, and what is the fix?
notes.back: Thread i reads p[i].x, so neighbouring threads are sizeof(struct) bytes apart: a strided, uncoalesced access. Structure of arrays (x[i], y[i], z[i]) makes each field contiguous.
notes.extra: In practice: this is the GPU version of the cache-line argument in 09; on a CPU AoS is often fine because one thread uses the whole struct. Link: 09 Memory · cache lines

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::10 GPU Architecture & Programming Model
notes.text: CUDA memory spaces: {{c1::global}} = device dynamic RAM (DRAM), visible to all blocks and the host; {{c2::shared}} = per-block on-chip scratchpad; {{c3::local}} = per-thread spills and indexed arrays, physically in global memory; {{c4::constant}} = 64 KB read-only, cached and broadcast.
notes.extra: Pitfall: constant memory is fast only when a warp reads the same address (one fetch broadcast); differing addresses serialise. Good for coefficients, bad for per-thread tables.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::10 GPU Architecture & Programming Model
notes.front: Why is a GPU's memory system built for bandwidth rather than latency?
notes.back: Thousands of resident warps generate thousands of outstanding requests, and the warp scheduler hides each one's latency; what limits throughput is bytes per second, hence wide high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and a large shared L2 that also resolves global atomics.
notes.extra: Link: Cloud Architecture · HBM, NVLink; 09 Memory · Little's law

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::10 GPU Architecture & Programming Model
notes.front: What does a tensor-core instruction such as parallel thread execution (PTX) mma.sync.m16n8k16 compute, and who issues it?
notes.back: A whole warp cooperatively computes D = A×B + C on a small tile (16×16 by 16×8 here), with fragments of A, B and C spread across the 32 threads' registers.
notes.extra: Why it matters: one instruction replaces thousands of scalar fused multiply-add operations (FMAs), so matmul throughput jumps an order of magnitude over CUDA cores. Link: 11 Accelerators · systolic array; bfloat16 & FP32 accumulation

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::10 GPU Architecture & Programming Model
notes.front: What are the stages from a .cu file to code running on the GPU?
notes.back: nvcc splits host and device code. Device code → PTX (virtual instruction set architecture (ISA)) → ptxas → NVIDIA's native GPU assembly (SASS) cubin for a specific streaming multiprocessor (SM); the host compiler builds the CPU side and the cubins/PTX are embedded as a fat binary.
notes.extra: Link: 03 IR & Optimisation · LLVM; 12 Mapping · PyTorch matmul path

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::10 GPU Architecture & Programming Model
notes.front: Parallel thread execution (PTX) vs NVIDIA's native GPU assembly (SASS): key difference?
notes.back: PTX: a stable, textual, virtual instruction set architecture (ISA) with unlimited virtual registers; forward-compatible across GPU generations. SASS: the real, undocumented machine code of one architecture, after register allocation and scheduling by ptxas.
notes.analogy: PTX is the LLVM IR of the GPU world; SASS is the x86 bytes.
notes.extra: In practice: cuobjdump -sass shows what actually runs; register spills and instruction mixes are only visible there.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::10 GPU Architecture & Programming Model
notes.front: NVIDIA's native GPU assembly (SASS) vs µops: does a GPU have a decode stage like a CPU's x86 → µop front end?
notes.back: Not in that sense. SASS is already a fixed-width, RISC-like instruction set architecture (ISA) the streaming multiprocessor (SM) issues directly, with dependency and stall counts written into control bits by ptxas at compile time. The CPU decodes and schedules at run time; the GPU moved that work into ptxas, so parallel thread execution (PTX) → SASS is its 'decode', done once.
notes.extra: Consequence: no µop cache, no renaming, no out-of-order on the SM; latency is hidden by switching warps instead. Link: 08 Microarchitecture · µop cache; scheduler; 10 GPU · latency hiding

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::10 GPU Architecture & Programming Model
notes.front: Why does a CUDA fat binary carry parallel thread execution (PTX) as well as NVIDIA's native GPU assembly (SASS) cubins?
notes.back: A cubin runs only on the compute capability it was built for. When a newer GPU has no matching cubin, the driver JIT-compiles the embedded PTX to its SASS at load time (and caches it on disk).
notes.extra: Example: -gencode arch=compute_80,code=[sm_80,compute_80] embeds both. Pitfall: cubin-only builds fail with 'no kernel image is available' on a newer card; every extra sm_XX target grows build time and binary size.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::10 GPU Architecture & Programming Model
notes.front: NVIDIA warp vs AMD wavefront: what differs, and why does it matter for ported code?
notes.back: Datacenter CDNA runs 64-wide wavefronts (RDNA gaming parts default to 32). Divergence and shuffle widths change, so code tuned for 32 lanes wastes lanes or reads the wrong neighbour; use warpSize, not 32.
notes.extra: In practice: Heterogeneous-computing Interface for Portability (HIP) is source-portable with CUDA (hipify), but tensor-core code (mma) must be rewritten against AMD's matrix fused multiply-add (MFMA) intrinsics.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::10 GPU Architecture & Programming Model
notes.front: Why do Apple and ARM mobile GPUs use tile-based deferred rendering (TBDR)?
notes.back: The screen is split into tiles that fit on-chip memory; all geometry is binned first, hidden surfaces removed, then each tile is shaded and written once. Framebuffer and depth traffic to dynamic RAM (DRAM), the main power cost, nearly disappears.
notes.extra: Contrast: desktop GPUs render immediately in draw order and rely on bandwidth. Pitfall: reading back the framebuffer mid-frame forces a tile flush and ruins the saving.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::10 GPU Architecture & Programming Model
notes.front: Why can 100,000 tiny kernel launches be slower than the same work on a CPU, and what do CUDA graphs change?
notes.back: Each launch costs a few microseconds of driver and queue work, so microsecond-sized kernels are overhead-bound. A graph captures the kernel/copy sequence once as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) and replays it as one launch, back to back on the GPU.
notes.extra: In practice: used by inference engines and torch.compile (mode reduce-overhead); only works when shapes and pointers are stable between replays.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::10 GPU Architecture & Programming Model
notes.front: What is a CUDA stream, and how does it give overlap?
notes.back: An in-order queue of kernels and copies. Different streams may run concurrently, so a copy for batch N+1 can overlap compute on batch N, provided the host memory is pinned and the GPU has free resources.
notes.analogy: Several checkout lanes: each lane serves customers in order, but lanes run in parallel.
notes.extra: Pitfall: the legacy default stream synchronises with every other stream, silently serialising a 'parallel' pipeline.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::10 GPU Architecture & Programming Model
notes.front: How does CUDA unified memory work, and when does it hurt?
notes.back: One pointer usable by CPU and GPU; pages migrate on demand via page faults. It hurts when both sides touch the same pages alternately (page ping-pong) or when a kernel first-touches gigabytes, each fault costing microseconds.
notes.extra: Fix: cudaMemPrefetchAsync and cudaMemAdvise hints, or explicit copies on a stream for the hot path.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::10 GPU Architecture & Programming Model
notes.front: Why are GPUs bad at branchy, pointer-chasing code such as tree walks?
notes.back: No branch predictor and lockstep warps mean every differing branch serialises lanes, and dependent loads cannot be overlapped within a thread; the only latency hiding is other warps, which the same code also stalls.
notes.extra: Link: 09 Memory · prefetchers

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::10 GPU Architecture & Programming Model
notes.front: A kernel runs 50× faster on the GPU than on the CPU, yet the program only gains 2×. Why?
notes.back: Amdahl's law: the serial parts (host preprocessing, Peripheral Component Interconnect Express (PCIe) copies, launch latency) now dominate. If they were 40% of the original time, the ceiling is 1/0.4 = 2.5× however fast the kernel.
notes.extra: In practice: keep data resident on the GPU across kernels, overlap copies with streams, and move the preprocessing onto the GPU too. Link: 12 Mapping · performance models

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::10 GPU Architecture & Programming Model
notes.front: How does a warp reduce 32 values without shared memory?
notes.back: Butterfly with __shfl_down_sync(mask, v, offset) for offsets 16, 8, 4, 2, 1: lanes exchange registers directly, five steps, no memory and no barrier.
notes.extra: Also: __ballot_sync gives a 32-bit mask of which lanes voted true, the basis of warp-level compaction and stream compaction.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::11 TPUs, AI Accelerators & their Compilers
notes.front: Why are AI accelerators built around matrix multiplication rather than general-purpose compute?
notes.back: Dense layers, convolutions and attention all reduce to matmuls, so one highly regular operation carries most of the floating-point operations (FLOPs) of training and inference.
notes.analogy: A bakery that sells 95% bread buys a bread oven, not a general kitchen.
notes.extra: In practice: everything that is not a matmul (softmax, layernorm, Gaussian error linear unit (GELU)) still needs a programmable vector unit next to the array.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::11 TPUs, AI Accelerators & their Compilers
notes.front: An accelerator has peak P floating-point operations per second (FLOP/s) and high-bandwidth memory (HBM) bandwidth B bytes/s. Which kernels on it are memory-bound, and what does that cover in practice?
notes.back: Every kernel whose arithmetic intensity (floating-point operations (FLOPs) per byte moved) is below the ridge point P/B, which on accelerators is hundreds of FLOP/byte: everything except large matmuls, i.e. elementwise ops, softmax, layernorm and batch-1 decode.
notes.analogy: Chewing per bite: a dish you must fetch a spoonful at a time is limited by the trips, not by your jaw.
notes.extra: Consequence: most of an accelerator compiler's work is raising intensity: fusion, tiling, keeping operands in static RAM (SRAM). Link: 09 Memory · Roofline

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::11 TPUs, AI Accelerators & their Compilers
notes.front: In a weight-stationary systolic array, which operand stays in the cells and which two flow?
notes.back: The weights are pre-loaded, one per cell. Activations stream in from one side (left) and partial sums flow through the perpendicular direction (down), accumulating per column.
notes.analogy: A bucket brigade: every person stands still, water (data) passes hand to hand, nobody walks back to the well.
notes.extra: Example: the tensor processing unit (TPU)'s matrix multiply unit (MXU). Each cell does one multiply-add per clock and hands results to its neighbour; Link: Cloud Architecture · systolic array intro

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::11 TPUs, AI Accelerators & their Compilers
notes.front: Why does a systolic array need no instruction fetch, register-file read or cache lookup per multiply-add, and why is that the whole point?
notes.back: Data moves register-to-register between neighbours on a fixed schedule; the dataflow is the program. The energy of a CPU/GPU multiply-accumulate (MAC) is dominated by exactly those overheads, not the arithmetic.
notes.extra: Link: 08 Microarchitecture · why in-order cores are cheap

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::11 TPUs, AI Accelerators & their Compilers
notes.front: Why are activation rows fed into a systolic array skewed by one cycle per row?
notes.back: Each cell must receive its activation at the same moment the partial sum from the cell above arrives. Row k therefore starts k cycles late; the array fills and drains like a pipeline.
notes.extra: Pitfall: fill/drain latency is wasted unless the next tile is already streaming in; the tensor processing unit (TPU) double-buffers weights so new weights load while the current ones compute.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::11 TPUs, AI Accelerators & their Compilers
notes.front: What breaks when the matrix you multiply is smaller than the systolic array (e.g. batch 1 decoding on a 128×128 matrix multiply unit (MXU))?
notes.back: The array is padded with zeros: utilisation collapses to (rows used ÷ 128). Each weight is loaded for one multiply instead of 128, so the step becomes memory-bound.
notes.analogy: A 128-seat bus making its route for one passenger.
