notes.extra: In practice: batching requests, or chips with smaller arrays / SRAM-resident weights, are the fixes. Link: LLMs deck · decode is memory-bound

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::11 TPUs, AI Accelerators & their Compilers
notes.text: A tensor processing unit (TPU) TensorCore has three kinds of unit: the {{c1::MXU (matrix unit, the systolic array)}} for matmuls, the {{c2::VPU (vector unit)}} for elementwise ops, reductions, activations and normalisation, and a {{c3::scalar unit}} that runs the control flow and issues instructions to the other two.
notes.extra: In practice: a kernel that is all softmax/layernorm leaves the MXU idle; Accelerated Linear Algebra (XLA)'s job is to keep the MXU fed and hide the VPU work under it.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::11 TPUs, AI Accelerators & their Compilers
notes.front: The matrix multiply unit (MXU) multiplies in bfloat16 but accumulates in FP32. Why that split?
notes.back: A multiplier's area grows roughly with the square of mantissa bits, so 8-bit mantissas make the array far denser; the adder chain is cheap, and 32-bit floating point (FP32) sums avoid losing small products over thousands of terms.
notes.extra: Same split on GPUs: tensor cores multiply FP16/BF16 fragments and accumulate in FP32 for the same reasons. Link: Cloud Architecture · BF16 vs FP16 range; 10 GPU · tensor-core MMA

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::11 TPUs, AI Accelerators & their Compilers
notes.front: Why is 8-bit integer (INT8) so attractive for inference hardware, and what must software add to make it work?
notes.back: Integer multipliers are much smaller and 8-bit values halve bandwidth versus brain floating point 16 (BF16). Software must supply a scale (and sometimes zero-point) per tensor or channel, chosen by calibration or training-aware quantisation.
notes.analogy: Shipping prices in whole cents with the currency noted once on the invoice: the unit (scale) travels separately from the numbers.
notes.extra: Link: LLMs deck · quantisation trade-off

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::11 TPUs, AI Accelerators & their Compilers
notes.front: 8-bit floating point (FP8) E4M3 vs E5M2: which goes where in training, and why?
notes.back: E4M3 (more mantissa, range ≈ ±448) for weights and activations, which need precision. E5M2 (more exponent, range ≈ ±57k) for gradients, which need range more than precision.
notes.extra: In practice: both still need a per-tensor 32-bit floating point (FP32) scale factor; the raw FP8 range is too small for most tensors.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::11 TPUs, AI Accelerators & their Compilers
notes.front: What is block (micro)scaling such as the Open Compute Project (OCP) MX formats, and what problem does it fix for FP8/FP4?
notes.back: A small block (e.g. 32 elements) shares one 8-bit exponent scale, so each element can be tiny (FP4/FP6/FP8) yet the block keeps useful dynamic range.
notes.analogy: A choir sheet with one key signature per bar instead of per note.
notes.extra: Trend: hardware reads the shared scale alongside the block, so the multiplier stays narrow while outliers no longer force a whole tensor to a coarse scale.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::11 TPUs, AI Accelerators & their Compilers
notes.front: On-chip SRAM vs HBM on an accelerator: what does each give, and what does the compiler do with the difference?
notes.back: Static RAM (SRAM): tens of MB, enormous bandwidth, low energy. High-bandwidth memory (HBM): tens of GB, ~10× less bandwidth and far more energy per byte. The compiler tiles work so the hot set lives in SRAM and HBM is streamed once.
notes.extra: Link: Cloud Architecture · HBM; 09 Memory · bandwidth vs latency

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::11 TPUs, AI Accelerators & their Compilers
notes.front: Why do accelerators use software-managed scratchpads instead of hardware caches like a CPU?
notes.back: Shapes and access patterns are known at compile time, so the compiler can schedule every transfer. Dropping tags, replacement logic and coherence saves area, energy and timing surprises.
notes.analogy: A chef who knows tonight's menu lays out ingredients in order (scratchpad); a diner with unknown orders keeps a fridge of likely items (cache).
notes.extra: Cost: dynamic shapes, data-dependent indexing (gather/scatter) and ragged batches become the compiler's problem instead of the hardware's.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::11 TPUs, AI Accelerators & their Compilers
notes.text: Accelerated Linear Algebra (XLA)'s pipeline: the framework emits {{c1::HLO}} (a graph of tensor ops with static shapes); target-independent passes simplify it (algebra, common subexpression elimination (CSE), dead-code elimination (DCE)); {{c2::layout assignment}} picks physical dimension orders and tiles; {{c3::fusion}} merges ops into kernels; {{c4::buffer assignment}} fixes every allocation at compile time; a backend (LLVM for CPU/GPU, the tensor processing unit (TPU) backend) emits machine code.
notes.extra: Link: 03 IR & Optimisation · pass pipeline

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::11 TPUs, AI Accelerators & their Compilers
notes.front: What does Accelerated Linear Algebra (XLA) fusion actually buy, and on which kind of op?
notes.back: It avoids writing intermediate tensors to high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and reading them back. For memory-bound elementwise chains (exp(x)*y + z) three kernels and three round-trips become one.
notes.analogy: Running all errands in one trip instead of coming home between shops.
notes.extra: Why it works: a matmul's intensity grows with size (~2N³ floating-point operations (FLOPs) on ~3N² values); an elementwise op's is fixed at ~1 FLOP/element, so fusing it into a matmul adds free FLOPs and removes a memory pass. Link: 09 Memory · Roofline; 08 Microarchitecture · µop fusion (contrast)

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::11 TPUs, AI Accelerators & their Compilers
notes.front: Compiler fusion (Accelerated Linear Algebra (XLA) / Inductor, 11) vs µop fusion (08): same word, what differs?
notes.back: Compiler fusion merges whole tensor ops into one kernel so intermediates never touch high-bandwidth memory (HBM): saves memory traffic, decided at compile time. µop fusion merges two adjacent instructions into one pipeline slot: saves front-end width, done by hardware per instruction. Opposite ends of the stack, same motive: remove an intermediate hand-off.
notes.extra: Link: 08 Microarchitecture · micro/macro-fusion; 09 Memory · Roofline

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::11 TPUs, AI Accelerators & their Compilers
notes.front: Why does Accelerated Linear Algebra (XLA) demand static shapes and compile ahead of time, and what does that cost the user?
notes.back: Static shapes let it choose tiles, pad to the hardware's lanes and fix every buffer at compile time, so the device never allocates or branches on sizes. Cost: a new shape means a recompile, so ragged data is bucketed or padded.
notes.extra: Contrast: eager PyTorch decides shapes at run time per op; torch.compile moves toward XLA's model with guards and symbolic shapes.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::11 TPUs, AI Accelerators & their Compilers
notes.front: How does jax.jit turn a Python function into a program, and why does print() inside it fire only once?
notes.back: It runs the Python once with abstract tracers (shape + dtype, no values), recording every JAX op into a jaxpr. Python-level side effects happen during that one trace; the compiled program later runs without Python.
notes.analogy: A choreographer walks through the dance once with stand-ins and writes down the steps; the performance never consults the choreographer again.
notes.extra: Pitfall: if x > 0: on a traced value raises an error; use lax.cond, or mark the argument static so each value gets its own trace.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::11 TPUs, AI Accelerators & their Compilers
notes.front: In Triton, what is the unit of programming, and how does that differ from CUDA?
notes.back: A Triton program handles a block (tile) of elements: pid = tl.program_id(0), then tl.load/tl.store on ranges with masks. CUDA programs a single thread; Triton's compiler decides how threads, coalescing and shared memory implement the tile.
notes.analogy: Ordering a wall built (block) vs instructing each bricklayer by hand (thread).
notes.extra: Link: 10 GPU · grid/block/warp mapping

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::11 TPUs, AI Accelerators & their Compilers
notes.front: Why must BLOCK_SIZE be a tl.constexpr in Triton?
notes.back: Tile sizes must be known at compile time so the compiler can size registers and shared memory, unroll loops and pick a warp layout. Each constexpr value compiles to a separate kernel.
notes.extra: In practice: autotuning simply tries several constexpr configs and keeps the fastest.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::11 TPUs, AI Accelerators & their Compilers
notes.front: What problem does multi-level intermediate representation (MLIR) solve that a single intermediate representation (IR) like LLVM IR cannot?
notes.back: One infrastructure for many dialects at different abstraction levels (tensor ops, loops, affine maps, GPU, LLVM), with progressive lowering between them. Tensor-level optimisations are impossible once everything is scalar LLVM IR.
notes.analogy: A building site with separate drawings for architecture, structure and plumbing, all in one CAD system, instead of only the wiring diagram.
notes.extra: Link: 03 IR & Optimisation · IR designs (LLVM / GIMPLE / MLIR)

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::11 TPUs, AI Accelerators & their Compilers
notes.text: A typical multi-level intermediate representation (MLIR) lowering for a matmul: {{c1::linalg}} (structured op with indexing maps: tile, fuse, vectorise here) → {{c2::affine / scf}} (explicit loops; affine maps allow polyhedral analysis of bounds and dependences) → {{c3::vector}} ops → {{c4::llvm}} dialect → LLVM intermediate representation (IR) → machine code.
notes.extra: Why the order: tiling on linalg.matmul is a one-line transform; recovering the same tiling from nested loops would need loop-nest analysis.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::11 TPUs, AI Accelerators & their Compilers
notes.front: Why is FlashAttention best understood as a compiler idea (tiling + fusion) rather than a new model?
notes.back: It computes exact attention in tiles that fit on-chip static RAM (SRAM), fusing QKᵀ, softmax and ×V so the n×n score matrix never touches high-bandwidth memory (HBM). The enabling trick is online softmax: rescaling running sums as new tiles arrive.
notes.extra: Why compilers missed it: the fusion needs an algebraic rewrite of softmax, not just loop reordering. Link: LLMs deck · FlashAttention

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::11 TPUs, AI Accelerators & their Compilers
notes.front: Groq-style deterministic dataflow accelerators: what does the compiler decide, and what disappears from the hardware?
notes.back: The compiler schedules every data movement to the clock cycle at compile time. The chip drops caches, branch predictors and dynamic schedulers; weights sit in on-chip static RAM (SRAM), so latency is exact and tiny.
notes.analogy: A railway timetable instead of road traffic: no lights, no jams, but every train was planned months ago.
notes.extra: Cost: SRAM is small, so one model spans many chips; the design suits inference, not training.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::11 TPUs, AI Accelerators & their Compilers
notes.front: Why does Cerebras build a wafer-scale chip, and what architectural model goes with it?
notes.back: Keeping hundreds of thousands of small cores and their static RAM (SRAM) on one wafer avoids the off-chip bandwidth wall between dies. Cores form a 2-D mesh with local memory; dataflow execution lets them skip multiplies by zero (sparsity).
notes.extra: In practice: weights for large models stream in from an external memory appliance (weight streaming); defective cores are routed around.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::11 TPUs, AI Accelerators & their Compilers
notes.front: Why does hardware accelerate only structured sparsity (e.g. 2:4), not arbitrary zeros in a weight matrix?
notes.back: With exactly 2 non-zeros per group of 4, a 2-bit index per value lets the multiply-accumulate (MAC) array fetch the matching activations and skip half the work with fixed-size metadata. Random sparsity needs irregular indexing that breaks the systolic flow.
notes.analogy: A parking garage with every other bay guaranteed empty is easy to size; random empty bays save nothing.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::11 TPUs, AI Accelerators & their Compilers
notes.front: Why are training chips designed differently from inference chips, in terms of arithmetic intensity?
notes.back: Training runs big batches: high intensity, compute-bound, needs 32-bit floating point (FP32) accumulation, memory for optimizer state and fast collectives. Inference (especially decode) reads every weight for little compute: low intensity, memory-bound, wants low precision and SRAM-near weights.
notes.extra: Link: Cloud Architecture · training vs inference chips

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::11 TPUs, AI Accelerators & their Compilers
notes.front: How does an ML compiler split one model across thousands of tensor processing unit (TPU) chips (Accelerated Linear Algebra (XLA)'s single program, multiple data (SPMD) partitioner / general and scalable parallelisation for ML computation graphs (GSPMD))?
notes.back: The user annotates how a few tensors are sharded across a device mesh; the partitioner propagates shardings through the high-level operations (HLO) graph and inserts collectives (all-reduce, all-gather) where ops need data another chip holds.
notes.extra: Why it matters: the same single-program source runs on 1 or 4096 chips; the compiler, not the model code, owns the communication.

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::12 From Source to Silicon: the Mapping
notes.text: The layer stack for for (i=0;i<n;i++) a[i]+=b[i];: front end makes {{c1::tokens and an AST}}; the middle end makes {{c2::SSA IR and optimises it (vectorise)}}; the back end emits {{c3::machine code in the ISA}}; the core turns it into {{c4::µops scheduled out of order}}; memory serves it in {{c5::64-byte cache lines}}.
notes.extra: Layers: 01–04 are software (the compiler), 06 is the contract, 08–09 are hardware. Each layer may rely only on what the one below promises. Link: 01 Parsing · AST; 03 IR & Optimisation · SSA; 06 x86-64 · AVX loop; 08 Microarchitecture · µops; 09 Memory · cache lines

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::12 From Source to Silicon: the Mapping
notes.front: Layer 01 (front end). What does the lexer and parser know about a[i] += b[i], and what does it not know?
notes.back: Knows the structure: a CompoundAssign(+=) node with two Subscript children inside a ForStmt. Does not yet know types, whether a is an array or pointer, or anything about cost.
notes.extra: Link: 01 Parsing · precedence & AST; 02 Types · symbol table

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::12 From Source to Silicon: the Mapping
notes.front: Layer 02 (semantics). How do types change what a[i] += b[i] means and compiles to?
notes.back: With int arrays it is an integer add (vpaddd); with float a float add (vaddps); mixing types inserts conversions. Signed overflow of i is undefined behaviour (UB), which lets the optimiser assume the loop terminates normally.
notes.extra: Link: 02 Types · UB in semantics; 03 IR & Optimisation · undef vs poison

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::12 From Source to Silicon: the Mapping
notes.front: Layer 03 (IR). What does the loop look like in static single assignment (SSA) form?
notes.back: Blocks: preheader (i₀ = 0) → header with i = φ(i₀, i₁) and the exit test → body (load a[i], load b[i], add, store) → latch (i₁ = i + 1) back to the header.
notes.extra: Link: 03 IR & Optimisation · SSA & φ; dominators

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::12 From Source to Silicon: the Mapping
notes.front: Layer 03 (optimisation). What must the compiler prove before it may vectorise a[i] += b[i] with 8-wide Advanced Vector Extensions 2 (AVX2)?
notes.back: That a and b do not overlap in a way that creates a loop-carried dependence. Without restrict it emits a runtime alias check and keeps a scalar fallback, plus a remainder loop for n % 8.
notes.analogy: Repainting eight fence boards at once is only safe if nobody is standing where you will swing.
notes.extra: Link: 03 IR & Optimisation · loop vectorisation & versioning; Deep C · restrict

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::12 From Source to Silicon: the Mapping
notes.front: Layer 04 (codegen). Which register-level decisions turn the vectorised intermediate representation (IR) into a tight loop?
notes.back: i lives in a register; strength reduction replaces a + i*4 with a running byte offset; register allocation gives the vector temporary a ymm; the exit test becomes cmp/jne.
notes.extra: Link: 04 Codegen & ABI · instruction selection; register allocation; 03 IR & Optimisation · strength reduction

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::12 From Source to Silicon: the Mapping
notes.front: Layer 06 (ISA). What does the hot Advanced Vector Extensions 2 (AVX2) loop body look like on x86-64?
notes.back:
.L: vmovdqu ymm0, [rsi+rax]
    vpaddd  ymm0, ymm0, [rdi+rax]
    vmovdqu [rdi+rax], ymm0
    add     rax, 32
    cmp     rax, rdx
    jne     .L
notes.extra: Reading it: one register rax indexes both arrays; 32 bytes = 8 ints per iteration. Link: 06 x86-64 · addressing modes; ymm registers

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::12 From Source to Silicon: the Mapping
notes.front: Layer 08 (microarchitecture). What happens to those six instructions inside the core?
notes.back: Decoded into µops: vpaddd with a memory operand micro-fuses load+add; cmp/jne macro-fuse into one µop. The loop lives in the µop cache, is renamed, runs out of order, and its branch is predicted taken until the exit mispredicts once.
notes.extra: Link: 08 Microarchitecture · micro/macro-fusion; µop cache; renaming

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::12 From Source to Silicon: the Mapping
notes.front: Layer 09 (memory). What bounds this loop, and how do you tell?
notes.back: Each iteration moves 96 bytes (two loads, one store) for 8 adds: ~0.08 FLOP/byte, far below any ridge point, so it is bandwidth-bound. Cache lines (64 B) are streamed by the hardware prefetcher; the core idles on memory.
notes.analogy: Eight people with one tiny door: the door, not the people, sets the pace.
notes.extra: Link: 09 Memory · prefetchers; Roofline; 11 Accelerators · fusion saves memory passes

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::12 From Source to Silicon: the Mapping
notes.front: Layer 07 (another ISA). Compile the same loop for AArch64 with Scalable Vector Extension (SVE): what changes below the intermediate representation (IR), and what does not?
notes.back: Same tokens, abstract syntax tree (AST), static single assignment (SSA) and vectorised IR. Below: fixed 32-bit instructions, predicated ld1w/add/st1w under a whilelt mask that also covers the tail (no remainder loop), incw stepping by the vector length. The binary never names the vector width.
notes.extra: Lesson: the instruction set architecture (ISA) layer decides the code's shape; every layer above it is shared across targets. Link: 07 ARM64/RISC-V/Z · SVE predication; 06 x86-64 · AVX-512 masking; 03 IR & Optimisation · loop vectorisation

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::12 From Source to Silicon: the Mapping
notes.front: JavaScript (JS), layer 05→06. How does an inline cache turn a.b into machine code?
notes.back: Ignition bytecode (GetNamedProperty a, [b], [slot]) records (hidden class → offset) in its feedback slot. When monomorphic, TurboFan emits: compare a's map with the cached one; on match load [a + offset]; on mismatch jump to a slow path or deoptimise.
notes.extra: What breaks: after a handful of shapes the site goes megamorphic: generic lookup, tens of times slower, and surrounding optimised code may deoptimise. Link: 05 Runtimes · inline caches; speculation & deopt; 08 Microarchitecture · branch prediction

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::12 From Source to Silicon: the Mapping
notes.front: C a.b vs JavaScript a.b: where is the field offset decided, and by whom?
notes.back: C: at compile time by the struct type: one mov [rdi+8], always. JS: at run time by observed hidden classes: a guarded load that is fast only while the guess holds.
notes.extra: Link: 02 Types · static vs dynamic typing; 05 Runtimes · speculation

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::12 From Source to Silicon: the Mapping
notes.front: Python, NumPy path. Which layers does a @ b cross before an Advanced Vector Extensions (AVX) instruction runs?
notes.back: Python bytecode → NumPy's C matmul ufunc → a Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms (BLAS) library (OpenBLAS/MKL) sgemm → hand-tuned, cache-blocked AVX-512/NEON micro-kernels, multithreaded. The interpreter is involved only at the top.
notes.extra: Lesson: interpreted glue around compiled kernels is fine when each call does millions of floating-point operations (FLOPs); it is fatal when it does ten. Link: 05 Runtimes · bytecode interpreter; 06 x86-64 · AVX; 09 Memory · cache blocking

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::12 From Source to Silicon: the Mapping
notes.front: Python, PyTorch eager path. What happens between a @ b on CUDA tensors and the GPU?
notes.back: ATen's dispatcher picks the CUDA/dtype kernel → cuBLAS is called → it launches a precompiled NVIDIA's native GPU assembly (SASS) kernel (shipped per compute capability, with parallel thread execution (PTX) fallback) on a stream; Python returns before the GPU finishes.
notes.extra: Link: 10 GPU · PTX vs SASS; streams; fat binaries

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::12 From Source to Silicon: the Mapping
notes.front: Python, compiled path. How does torch.compile change the route to the GPU?
notes.back: Dynamo traces the Python into an FX graph → Inductor fuses elementwise ops and emits Triton kernels → Triton → LLVM → parallel thread execution (PTX) → ptxas → NVIDIA's native GPU assembly (SASS). Matmuls are autotuned among cuBLAS, Triton and CUTLASS candidates.
notes.extra: Vs eager: one launch per op and every intermediate in high-bandwidth memory (HBM) become fused kernels with intermediates in registers; the price is compile time and shape guards. Link: 11 Accelerators · Triton; fusion; 10 GPU · launch overhead & CUDA graphs

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::12 From Source to Silicon: the Mapping
notes.front: Python, TPU path. Which layers does a @ b cross under jax.jit on a TPU?
notes.back: Tracing → jaxpr → high-level operations (HLO) → XLA (layout tiles, fusion, static buffer assignment) → tensor processing unit (TPU) backend → an instruction stream for the scalar unit that drives the matrix multiply unit (MXU) systolic array and the vector processing unit (VPU). No hand-written kernel anywhere: the compiler owns every byte moved.
notes.extra: Contrast: the eager CUDA path ends in cuBLAS kernels written by hand; the TPU path is compiled end to end. Link: 11 Accelerators · JAX tracing; XLA pipeline; MXU / VPU / scalar unit

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::12 From Source to Silicon: the Mapping
notes.front: What is the hardware/software contract, and which layer defines it?
notes.back: The ISA (layer 06): the compiler may assume exactly the documented effect of each instruction on architectural state; the hardware may implement it any way it likes (µops, speculation, caches) as long as that state matches.
notes.analogy: A restaurant menu: you may rely on what the dish is, not on how the kitchen is organised.
notes.extra: Example: the same binary runs on an in-order Cortex-A5x and on a very wide Apple core because both honour the contract. Link: 08 Microarchitecture · ISA vs microarchitecture; 06 x86-64 · the ISA

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::12 From Source to Silicon: the Mapping
notes.text: What each layer may assume: a C program may assume only the {{c1::abstract machine (anything else is UB)}}; the compiler may assume {{c2::ISA semantics and the ABI}}; the CPU may reorder freely as long as {{c3::a single thread sees program order}}; other threads are promised only what the {{c4::memory model}} says.
notes.extra: Link: 02 Types · UB; 04 Codegen & ABI · ABI vs API; 09 Memory · memory models; Deep C · barriers x86 vs ARM

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::12 From Source to Silicon: the Mapping
notes.front: Why is Spectre best described as a breach of the layer contract rather than a bug in one layer?
notes.back: The instruction set architecture (ISA) never promised timing; speculation keeps architectural state correct yet leaves cache-state footprints. Software that assumed 'unexecuted code has no effect' relied on something no layer guaranteed.
notes.extra: Link: 08 Microarchitecture · Spectre v1; Spectre v2 vs Meltdown; 09 Memory · cache timing

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::12 From Source to Silicon: the Mapping
notes.text: Where abstractions leak: fast on sorted, slow on random data → {{c1::branch mispredict}} (08); a cliff at a size threshold → {{c2::cache misses}} (09); a 'working' program changes with -O2 → {{c3::UB}} (02/03); periodic stalls → {{c4::GC pauses}} (05); branchy GPU kernels at half speed → {{c5::warp divergence}} (10).
notes.extra: Use: each symptom names the layer to blame, so you profile with that layer's tool (perf counters, cache stats, undefined behaviour sanitizer (UBSan), garbage collection (GC) logs, Nsight). Link: 08 Microarchitecture · branch prediction; 09 Memory · cache lines; 05 Runtimes · GC pauses; 10 GPU · divergence

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::12 From Source to Silicon: the Mapping
notes.front: Which layer do you blame: a service is fast, then stalls for tens of ms every few seconds, with CPU idle during the stall?
notes.back: The runtime (05): a stop-the-world garbage collection (GC) pause or just-in-time (JIT) deoptimisation storm. Check GC logs before touching the algorithm or the hardware.
notes.extra: Contrast: a stall with CPU busy points at a lock-free spin or a cache-thrashing phase (09). Link: 05 Runtimes · stop-the-world pauses; deopt storms

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::12 From Source to Silicon: the Mapping
notes.front: Which layer do you blame: the same loop is 4× slower once the array passes a few MB, with no change in instruction count?
notes.back: The memory hierarchy (09): the working set fell out of L2/L3 into dynamic RAM (DRAM). Instructions per cycle (IPC) drops, cache-miss counters rise; the fix is blocking or a smaller/denser data layout.
notes.extra: Link: 09 Memory · latency numbers; Roofline; 11 Accelerators · tiling for SRAM

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::12 From Source to Silicon: the Mapping
notes.front: Which layer do you blame: a program is 30% slower after a compiler upgrade, same source, same machine?
notes.back: The compiler layers (03/04): a changed inlining or vectorisation decision, different loop alignment or code layout, or a newly exploited piece of undefined behaviour (UB). Hardware and runtime did not change. Diff the two -O2 outputs on Compiler Explorer and read -Rpass-missed.
notes.extra: Pitfall: 'slower' may be i-cache layout (09) rather than instruction count; compare instructions retired and instructions per cycle (IPC) with perf stat. Link: 03 IR & Optimisation · inlining heuristics; reading -O2 output; 08 Microarchitecture · Top-Down

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::12 From Source to Silicon: the Mapping
notes.text: Performance mental models and their layer: {{c1::IPC}} measures how well the core (08) is fed; {{c2::Roofline}} tells whether a kernel is compute- or memory-bound (09, 11); {{c3::Amdahl's law}} bounds speed-up by the serial fraction (any parallel layer, 10); {{c4::latency vs throughput}} decides whether to optimise one request's path or the pipeline's width.
notes.extra: Link: 08 Microarchitecture · Top-Down; 09 Memory · Roofline; 10 GPU · Amdahl

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::12 From Source to Silicon: the Mapping
notes.front: Latency vs throughput: how does the choice change what you optimise at each layer?
notes.back: Latency (one request fast): shorten the critical path: fewer dependent loads, avoid misses and mispredicts, batch size 1. Throughput (many per second): widen the pipeline: batching, SIMD/SIMT, more in-flight work, accept per-item delay.
notes.analogy: An ambulance vs a freight train: both move things; you design the road differently.
notes.extra: Example: LLM decode at batch 1 is a latency problem (SRAM-near weights win); training is a throughput problem (big systolic arrays win). See 11. Link: 11 Accelerators · training vs inference; 10 GPU · latency hiding

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::12 From Source to Silicon: the Mapping
notes.front: Three 'intermediate instruction sets': bytecode (05), parallel thread execution (PTX) (10), microcode (08). Who produces each, who consumes it, and on which side of the instruction set architecture (ISA) does it sit?
notes.back:
• Bytecode: compiler → interpreter/JIT; above the ISA, portable, visible to the program.
  • PTX: compiler → ptxas or driver just-in-time (JIT) → NVIDIA's native GPU assembly (SASS); a virtual ISA above the real one.
  • Microcode: CPU vendor → the core's sequencer; below the ISA, invisible to software.
notes.analogy: A recipe in the cookbook (bytecode), the recipe adapted for your oven (PTX), and the oven's own firmware (microcode).
notes.extra: Lesson: all three are 'instructions', but only the ISA is the contract; the others are compiled down to it or hidden beneath it. Link: 05 Runtimes · stack vs register VM; 10 GPU · PTX vs SASS; 08 Microarchitecture · µop vs microcode

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::12 From Source to Silicon: the Mapping
notes.front: Under the stack: virtualisation. How do Intel Virtual Machine Extensions (VMX), AMD Secure Virtual Machine (SVM) and IBM's start interpretive execution (SIE) let a guest OS run unmodified on the real instruction set architecture (ISA)?
notes.back: The CPU adds a guest mode (VMX non-root / SVM guest / SIE interpretive execution) in which sensitive instructions and events exit to the hypervisor, with guest state saved in a control block (virtual machine control structure (VMCS) / virtual machine control block (VMCB) / state description). Nested page tables translate guest-physical to host-physical.
notes.analogy: A flight simulator cockpit: the pilot uses real controls, but certain switches quietly route to the instructor's console.
notes.extra: Layer: below the OS, above the ISA; the guest's compiler-generated code is unchanged. IBM shipped SIE in the 1980s; x86 caught up two decades later. Link: 07 ARM64/RISC-V/Z · SIE; RISC-V privilege levels; Linux Internals · page tables

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::12 From Source to Silicon: the Mapping
notes.front: Confidential computing (AMD SEV-SNP, Intel Trust Domain Extensions (TDX)): what changes in the trust layering compared with ordinary virtualisation?
notes.back: The hypervisor still schedules the VM but is untrusted: guest memory is encrypted with per-VM keys held by hardware, integrity is checked, and remote attestation proves to the tenant which firmware/guest image is running.
notes.extra: Layer: a hardware root of trust sits below the hypervisor; the instruction set architecture (ISA) contract now includes 'the host cannot read this memory'. Link: Cloud Architecture · shared-responsibility model

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::12 From Source to Silicon: the Mapping
notes.text: What the compiler cannot do for you: it will not change your {{c1::data structures or layout (AoS → SoA, pointer chasing → arrays)}}, your {{c2::algorithmic complexity}}, or add {{c3::parallelism across threads or devices}}; it cannot know {{c4::aliasing or value ranges you did not state}}, and it will not save code that relies on {{c5::undefined behaviour}}.
notes.extra: Why: each needs a guarantee that lives in a layer above the compiler (your intent, your data), or would change observable behaviour. Link: 09 Memory · cache lines; 03 IR & Optimisation · alias analysis; 02 Types · UB

notes.deck: From Source to Silicon::12 From Source to Silicon: the Mapping
notes.front: Why can't the compiler turn an array of structs into a struct of arrays for you, even when that would make the loop vectorise?
notes.back: Layout is part of the type's observable contract: pointers, sizeof, I/O and other translation units all see it. Changing it needs whole-program knowledge and a guarantee nobody casts or serialises the bytes.
notes.analogy: A librarian cannot re-shelve books by colour while readers hold call numbers.
notes.extra: Link: 03 IR & Optimisation · optimisation levels; 09 Memory · cache lines; 11 Accelerators · XLA layout assignment
